3.q: A team identifies all the key deliverables that must be placed under version control. Which configuration management activity is this?
o: Verification audit
Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
3.w: Configuration identification determines which items are to be controlled and labels them so they can be managed.

3.q: A project manager revises the likelihood rating of an existing risk after new information arrives. Where is this recorded?
o: In the project issue log
In the stakeholder register
In the risk register
In the schedule baseline
3.w: The risk register is kept up to date throughout the project to reflect changes in likelihood, impact and status.

3.q: A quality control check finds that several components fail to meet the specification; what should happen next?
o: Ignore the failures because most components passed
Adjust the original scope to match the output
Change the requirements to suit the output
Report the failure and decide on corrective action
3.w: Non-conformance found in quality control should be reported so that corrective action can be taken to meet the standard.

3.q: Following project handover, who is normally accountable for tracking whether the intended benefits are actually realised?
o: The project sponsor or designated benefits owner
The finance administrator who managed the budget
The lead supplier who provided the deliverables
The project manager who led the delivery work
3.w: Benefits are usually realised after the project has closed, so accountability passes to the sponsor or a designated benefits owner identified in the business case.

3.q: A team member regularly offers original, unorthodox ideas and creative solutions during workshops. Which Belbin role best describes them?
o: Completer Finisher
Team Worker
Plant
Shaper
3.w: The Plant is the creative thinker who generates novel ideas and imaginative solutions to the team's problems.

3.q: A key risk recorded in the project's risk register has now materialised. What should happen next?
o: It should be ignored because it has already been analysed
It should be closed and recorded as a completed milestone
It should be deleted from the risk register without further action
It should be reclassified as an issue and managed accordingly
3.w: Once a risk actually occurs it becomes a current problem, so it is reclassified as an issue and handled through the issue management process.

3.q: A sponsor wants a quick, high-level estimate based on a similar project completed last year. Which method should be used?
o: Analytical estimating
Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
3.w: Analogous estimating uses data from a comparable past project to give a fast, high-level estimate.

3.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between progress reporting and stakeholder confidence?
o: Frequent reports remove the need for stakeholder input
Clear, honest reports build trust and transparency
Reports should be withheld to avoid raising concerns
Reporting is the main cause of project scope creep
3.w: Transparent and honest reporting keeps stakeholders informed and engaged, which builds trust and confidence in the project.

3.q: Early feedback on a new IT system shows that users are confused by the interface wording. Which action best supports successful adoption?
o: Reassign the technical work to the users themselves
Transfer the concern to the sponsor as a risk
Arrange further end user engagement and training
Update the project governance plan
3.w: Engaging and training end users after handover helps embed the solution and maximise the benefits realised.

3.q: A client requests an urgent change to a critical deliverable. What should the project manager do first?
o: Implement the change straight away to meet expectations
Include the change within the next routine progress report
Email the project team and proceed with it immediately
Raise and assess a change request through the formal procedure
3.w: Every change, however urgent, is raised and assessed through the formal change control procedure so its impact is understood before any decision.

3.q: Which of the following best describes the role of success criteria at project handover?
o: They determine which team members remain on the project
They confirm that the business case is now obsolete
They serve as a benchmark for confirming that objectives have been met
They replace the need for a final project report
3.w: At handover, success criteria provide the measurable benchmark against which project outcomes are evaluated.

3.q: Which of the following is most likely to be included in a project communication plan?
o: A list of the sponsors of previous, unrelated projects
Escalation routes for unresolved communication issues
The individual salaries of the project team members
The technical hardware specifications of the deliverables
3.w: A communication plan commonly sets out how communication issues are escalated if they cannot be resolved.

3.q: What is a benefit of using email for communication on a project?
o: It is always a fully secure and completely private channel
It provides a written trail that can be referred to later
It functions without any need for an internet connection
It removes the need to hold project meetings altogether
3.w: Email creates an auditable written record that is easy to store and refer back to throughout the project.

3.q: A stakeholder raises a formal complaint during a project review meeting. Which process is used to handle this?
o: Scope management
Risk identification
Configuration management
Issue management
3.w: A complaint is a current concern that has arisen, so it is captured and addressed through the issue management process.

3.q: A team agrees its delivery scope, timeline and budget, and this is recorded and approved before work begins. What has been established?
o: A procurement strategy
A risk threshold
A communication plan
A deployment baseline
3.w: An agreed and approved reference for scope, time and cost before execution describes the deployment baseline.

3.q: What information is typically contained within a formal project progress report?
o: A complete list of the project's suppliers
Progress against plan, key risks, issues and forecast to complete
A post-project analysis of the benefits realised
The scope baseline and a full stakeholder map
3.w: A progress report typically sets out current status against the plan, key risks and issues, and a forecast of the outcome.

3.q: What key benefit does effective scheduling provide to a project manager?
o: Improved levels of motivation across the project team
Easier negotiation with influential project stakeholders
Reduced financial risk within the project business case
Clarity on task dependencies and the overall project duration
3.w: Scheduling makes dependencies visible and establishes how long the project will take, supporting sound planning and control.

3.q: What key function does the deployment baseline serve in relation to change control?
o: It sets the duration of the supplier contract
It provides a reference point for evaluating proposed changes
It guarantees that no changes will ever be permitted
It allows stakeholders to be removed without approval
3.w: All proposed changes are compared against the baseline so their impact can be assessed and approval sought.

3.q: Which scenario best illustrates poor stakeholder engagement caused by inadequate analysis?
o: A key regulator halted work because it was not consulted during planning
A quality report was produced in the wrong format
A supplier failed to deliver a component on time
The team did not complete the project risk register
3.w: Overlooking a key regulator during analysis and engagement planning can lead to serious blocks on delivery.

3.q: A software defect has been fixed, tested and verified. What is the final step in the issue resolution process?
o: Escalation of the issue to a higher authority
Closure of the issue, recording it as complete
Reassessment of the issue's potential impact
Reopening the issue for further investigation
3.w: Once an issue has been resolved and verified, it is formally closed and recorded as complete.

3.q: Which of the following is most likely to make it harder for a project manager to develop team cohesion?
o: Frequent changes in team membership
Consistent leadership behaviour over time
Early engagement in team development
Shared values and common goals
3.w: Frequent membership changes disrupt trust and progress through the team's development stages, making cohesion harder to build.

3.q: How does effective risk management benefit a project?
o: It shifts every decision onto the individual team members
It reduces the impact of threats and helps exploit opportunities
It removes all uncertainty from the project environment
It allows the project to ignore its business case
3.w: Managing risk reduces the effect of threats and helps the project take advantage of opportunities, improving the chance of success.

3.q: A team decides to take no pre-emptive action against a possible delay to key components. Which risk response is this?
o: Transfer
Acceptance
Avoidance
Mitigation
3.w: Acceptance means acknowledging a risk and taking no pre-emptive action unless it actually materialises.

3.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a project milestone?
o: To track the unresolved risks within the project
To assign specific tasks to individual project team members
To measure product quality against the baseline specification
To mark a significant point or achievement within the schedule
3.w: Milestones are zero-duration events that flag key points such as phase completions or major approvals within the schedule.

3.q: In a linear life cycle, a board reviews whether the project should move into its next phase; what is this review called?
o: A stakeholder review
A decision gate
A post-project review
A formal quality audit
3.w: A decision gate is a review point used to decide whether a project should proceed to the next phase.

3.q: Your project is one of eight coordinated under a wider business change programme. What is the role of programme management here?
o: To coordinate and align related projects for greater benefit
To focus only on your project's budget and schedule
To monitor health and safety across the organisation
To take over the duties of the individual project sponsors
3.w: Programme management coordinates and aligns related projects so they contribute to wider, shared business benefits.

3.q: A development team is waiting for its next batch of prioritised work. Who is responsible for keeping the backlog updated and correctly ordered?
o: The project manager
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
3.w: The product owner maintains the backlog and ensures the most valuable items are ready for the team to develop.

3.q: Early in the design phase a team produces an estimate with a tolerance of around plus or minus 40%. What does this represent in the estimating funnel?
o: A confirmed contingency figure
A final, validated estimate
A preliminary, high-level estimate
A detailed bottom-up estimate
3.w: Wide tolerances such as plus or minus 40% are typical of the preliminary, high-level estimates near the top of the funnel.

3.q: A newly formed project team is polite but hesitant and unsure of its direction. According to Tuckman's model, what should the leader mainly do?
o: Encourage members to work independently straight away
Avoid setting expectations to see how the team develops
Step back and let the team organise itself immediately
Provide clear direction and define the team's goals and roles
3.w: In the forming stage the team looks to the leader for direction and structure to build its early confidence.

3.q: Stakeholder analysis shows a group of community residents to have low influence but high interest. What is the recommended approach?
o: Avoid all engagement until after delivery
Monitor them only if they raise a concern
Manage them closely and involve them in every decision
Keep them informed through regular updates and consultation
3.w: Low-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be kept informed to maintain support and prevent misinformation.

4.q: What is the role of configuration management once a scope change has been formally approved?
o: To carry out the approval of the original change request
To redefine the project's chosen life cycle for delivery
To ensure the approved change is applied and documented correctly
To communicate the approved change out to the stakeholders
4.w: After change control approves a change, configuration management ensures it is implemented, recorded and reflected in the controlled products.

4.q: Which configuration management activity ensures that only approved changes are made to configuration items?
o: Configuration planning
Configuration identification
Status accounting
Configuration control
4.w: Configuration control ensures that changes to controlled items follow the correct review and approval process before being made.

4.q: A leader creates an environment where team members feel trusted and encouraged to share ideas. What is this most likely to improve?
o: Team performance and innovation
The quality of the risk register
The accuracy of the project budget
The logistics of the project location
4.w: Trust and inclusion encourage collaboration and allow teams to perform at their best.

4.q: A new member joins a project team midway through, tension rises and productivity dips. What should the project leader do?
o: Return to team-building activity to rebuild cohesion
Give the new member only isolated tasks to do
Ignore it and expect the team to settle itself
Remove the new member from the team at once
4.w: Adding a member can cause the team to regress, so the leader should revisit norming activities to restore cohesion.

4.q: Why is it important to tailor progress reports to different stakeholder groups?
o: To provide information relevant to each group's interest and influence
To remove the need for formal governance meetings
To avoid carrying out any project audits
To reduce the amount of communication within the team
4.w: Stakeholders have differing interests and influence, so tailoring reports ensures each group receives meaningful and relevant information.

4.q: A senior user reviews the project management plan and questions the schedule. Why is their involvement important?
o: They represent end-user needs and shape quality expectations
They manage all of the third-party procurement
They are accountable for allocating project risk
They take over the project manager's role if delays occur
4.w: Senior users ensure the plan reflects business needs and the quality expectations of those who will use the deliverables.

4.q: Which statement best defines a 'risk' in the context of project management?
o: A confirmed problem that requires immediate resolution by the team
An uncertain event that, should it occur, would affect the project's objectives
A completed task that is currently waiting for formal approval
A cost overrun that has already occurred and cannot be recovered
4.w: A risk is an uncertain future event that may have a positive or negative effect on project objectives.

4.q: A project manager regularly shares the vision, encourages initiative and supports team learning. Which leadership quality is being demonstrated?
o: Inspirational leadership that aligns the team
Purely reactive decision-making
Detailed cost and budget management
A command-and-control leadership style
4.w: Inspirational leaders energise and align their teams around a shared sense of purpose.

4.q: What is one benefit of applying a standard estimating funnel across an organisation's projects?
o: It replaces the need for bottom-up estimating
It fixes all estimates at the start of each project
It promotes consistent refinement of estimates across project phases
It removes the need for any contingency planning
4.w: A standard funnel provides a consistent approach to refining estimates as knowledge grows, aiding comparison across projects.

4.q: Which of the following best illustrates a risk on a project?
o: The project sponsor has already resigned from their post
A key supplier has already defaulted on an agreed delivery
The team has already exceeded the budget agreed for the phase
Adverse weather could delay the construction work later in the year
4.w: Adverse weather is an uncertain future event that may delay delivery, so it is a risk; the others have already happened and are issues.

4.q: What is a key benefit of summarising a verbal discussion in a follow-up email?
o: It guarantees the eventual success of the whole project
It removes the need for the original discussion to take place
It removes every possibility of the message being misread
It provides a record of what was agreed and the next steps
4.w: A written summary creates a record and reinforces shared understanding of what was agreed verbally.

4.q: An audit confirms that versioning rules were followed and only approved changes were made. What does this outcome confirm?
o: That all of the planned benefits have been realised
That the stakeholder requirements have changed
That the agreed project baseline has since changed
That configuration control and verification were effective
4.w: A satisfactory audit demonstrates that changes were properly controlled and that items conform to their approved configuration.

4.q: What distinguishes a project management office from a project manager?
o: The PMO provides oversight and tools across projects, while the manager delivers one project
The PMO reports to the project manager on each project by default
The PMO owns every work package, while the manager owns the schedule
The PMO leads stakeholder engagement, while the manager owns governance
4.w: The PMO supports governance and consistency across projects, while the project manager is accountable for delivering a specific project.

4.q: What is a key limitation of using email as a communication method?
o: It is the most suitable channel for urgent decision-making
It is not actually a written form of communication
It lacks tone and non-verbal cues, so it can be misread
It always ensures an immediate two-way exchange of views
4.w: Emails can be misinterpreted because they carry no tone of voice or body language.

4.q: An executive secured the funding and holds overall accountability for delivering the project's benefits. Which role is being described?
o: End user
Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
4.w: The project sponsor owns the business case, secures funding and is accountable for the realisation of the benefits.

4.q: How does leadership differ from management within a project environment?
o: Leadership focuses on scheduling, while management inspires the team
Leadership sets the vision and direction, while management ensures delivery
Leadership handles procurement, while management handles risk
Leadership and management are effectively identical in project delivery
4.w: Leadership provides vision and inspires others, whereas management concentrates on planning, control and execution.

4.q: A project manager arranges a backup supplier agreement in case the main vendor fails to deliver. Which risk response is this?
o: Risk acceptance
Risk transfer
Contingency planning
Risk avoidance
4.w: Preparing a fallback to be used only if the risk occurs is a contingency (fallback) response.

4.q: In the early stages of a project, who is primarily responsible for justifying the investment and championing the business case?
o: The PMO analyst
The delivery team member
The project sponsor
The project manager
4.w: The sponsor owns the business case, ensures alignment with strategic objectives and secures the funding.

4.q: What challenge might a project manager face when leading a team spread across multiple geographic locations?
o: Standardising tools that are already uniform everywhere
Reducing over-involvement from the team
Reconciling differing cultures and communication styles
Coping with excessive face-to-face interaction
4.w: Differences in culture and communication style can cause misunderstanding and tension, requiring the leadership approach to be tailored.

4.q: Partway through a project the team resolves its own disagreements and no longer needs frequent check-ins. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Performing
Norming
Forming
Storming
4.w: A performing team is mature and self-regulating, working effectively with minimal supervision from the leader.

4.q: What is the primary purpose of quality control within a project?
o: To document the interests of the stakeholders
To confirm outputs conform to specifications through inspection
To produce a detailed and costed business case
To manage the contracts held with suppliers
4.w: Quality control verifies outputs through inspection, measurement and testing to confirm they meet requirements.

4.q: Which of the following would typically be discussed during a post-project review?
o: Lessons learned and performance against objectives
Plans for procuring brand new suppliers
Estimates for the costs of a new product
Detailed technical rework of the product
4.w: Post-project reviews cover overall performance, stakeholder feedback and lessons learned to inform future projects.

4.q: An agile team reviews scope at the start of each sprint and updates priorities from user feedback. How does this reflect iterative scope management?
o: The deliverables are set upfront and reviewed only monthly
The product evolves through ongoing review and stakeholder input
The team proceeds without defining any scope at all
The scope is fixed at the start and is never revisited
4.w: In iterative projects the scope evolves as work progresses, guided by continual review and stakeholder feedback.

4.q: A risk plan notes that poor weather may delay construction. What benefit does identifying this early provide?
o: It removes the impact of every environmental risk on the project
It gives the team time to prepare responses before any delay occurs
It removes the need for configuration control during the project
It guarantees that the project will remain within its agreed scope
4.w: Identifying risks early is the purpose of risk management: it allows responses to be planned before problems arise.

4.q: A complex product must be delivered by combined IT and engineering teams. Which action best demonstrates project management?
o: Applying methods and tools to plan, execute and control delivery
Hiring additional administrative staff for routine services
Documenting every staff role across the whole organisation
Processing staff annual leave requests through a central team
4.w: Applying structured methods, processes and tools to plan and control the delivery is the essence of project management.

4.q: What is the main purpose of risk management on a project?
o: To improve the chance of meeting objectives by managing uncertainty
To replace the need for a project management plan
To transfer all responsibility for the project to the sponsor
To eliminate every possible risk before the project begins
4.w: Risk management aims to increase the likelihood of achieving objectives by identifying and responding to uncertainty, not to remove all risk.

4.q: A construction project introduced quality procedures early and monitored them regularly; what benefit does this bring?
o: It removes the need to obtain stakeholder approval
It increases the likelihood that deliverables meet their specifications
It guarantees that no changes will occur during delivery
It reduces the amount of planning the team must do
4.w: Applying quality management consistently helps ensure deliverables meet agreed specifications and reduces the likelihood of rework.

4.q: Critical path analysis shows a task that can be delayed without affecting the overall project timeline. What is this an example of?
o: Float
Budget slippage
Configuration drift
Scope creep
4.w: Float, or slack, is the amount of time an activity can be delayed without affecting the project's completion date.

4.q: During delivery, a scope change is identified that will affect cost and schedule. What is the first step the project manager should take?
o: Continue as planned and ignore the change
Reassign the work without recording it
Compare the proposed change against the deployment baseline
Notify stakeholders that the project will close
4.w: Proposed changes are first assessed against the deployment baseline to determine their impact and whether approval is required.

4.q: A team is given two weeks to complete as much as possible from a defined set of features. Which technique is being used?
o: Critical path calculation
Time boxing
Milestone tracking
Float analysis
4.w: This is time boxing: the duration is fixed at two weeks while the scope achieved within it is allowed to vary.

5.q: A quality assurance review shows that a key process is not being applied consistently; what should happen next?
o: The findings should be ignored by the team
The project should be closed down immediately
Corrective actions should be identified and implemented
The product should be delivered without change
5.w: Quality assurance identifies process shortfalls so that corrective actions can realign work with quality standards.

5.q: How do a product breakdown structure and a work breakdown structure support scope definition when used together?
o: They set out the project's risks and outstanding issues
They identify the communication channels and reporting lines
They link the deliverables to the work required to produce them
They record the financial transactions made for the stakeholders
5.w: Together the PBS and WBS connect what must be delivered to the work required to deliver it, giving a complete view of scope.

5.q: Stakeholders disagree over the project's success criteria partway through delivery. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Proceed with the original criteria and ignore the concerns
Revise and agree updated criteria through change control
Suspend all activity until full consensus is achieved
Replace the success criteria with the business case
5.w: Success criteria may need revising as expectations evolve, and any change should be agreed through the formal change control process.

5.q: While revising the project management plan, a project manager notices there has been no input from the senior supplier. What risk does this pose?
o: Delivery capability and logistics could be misaligned
The project may receive excessive funding
Stakeholder interest will rise unexpectedly
The benefits are likely to be over-delivered
5.w: Without supplier input the plan's delivery logistics may be unrealistic or misaligned with the supplier's capacity.

5.q: What is a downside of relying too heavily on informal verbal communication?
o: It guarantees that information is always communicated accurately
Agreements may go undocumented and be misunderstood later
It removes the need for any defined escalation routes
It substantially increases the volume of project documentation
5.w: Informal verbal communication relies on memory, so agreements can be forgotten or misunderstood unless confirmed in writing.

5.q: Keeping a logistics project aligned to the sponsor's strategic vision is best described as an example of what?
o: One of the fundamental purposes of project management
A post-project review conducted after handover
A portfolio management responsibility above the project
A quality assurance activity carried out independently
5.w: Ensuring the project stays aligned to organisational strategy and the sponsor's objectives is a core purpose of project management.

5.q: A project has quality procedures in place but never reviews whether the team follows them; what is missing?
o: Risk management activity
Scope management activity
Issue control activity
Quality assurance of processes
5.w: Without checks to verify process adherence, quality assurance is not being properly implemented.

5.q: Which of the following is a key advantage of face-to-face communication on a project?
o: It removes any need for written follow-up or documentation
It reduces the travel and scheduling costs for the team
It permits immediate feedback and the reading of body language
It guarantees that stakeholders will agree with the message
5.w: Face-to-face communication conveys non-verbal cues and allows misunderstandings to be clarified immediately.

5.q: What is a key difference in how deployment baselines are managed in linear versus iterative life cycles?
o: Linear projects avoid the use of baselines completely
Linear projects rely on a fixed baseline, while iterative projects expect it to evolve
Iterative life cycles set one baseline and never change it
Both approaches exclude stakeholders from creating the baseline
5.w: Linear life cycles seek stability through a fixed baseline, whereas iterative life cycles embrace an evolving one.

5.q: Which of the following best describes the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing specialist skills and completing assigned tasks
Defining and owning the project business case
Approving transitions between project phases
Authorising procurement contracts with suppliers
5.w: Team members apply their specialist skills to complete assigned work packages and report progress to the project manager.

5.q: Why can face-to-face communication be less effective in certain project delivery environments?
o: It provides too much written documentation for the team
It can be impractical for dispersed teams or tight schedules
It excludes body language from the exchange of information
It removes the need to consider cultural sensitivities
5.w: For geographically dispersed or fast-moving projects, arranging in-person meetings can be costly and time-consuming.

5.q: A benefit review finds that only part of the forecast savings were achieved; what should the organisation do?
o: Analyse why the benefits were not fully realised
Treat the whole project as a complete failure
Cancel all future benefit reviews entirely
Ignore the results because the project has closed
5.w: The gap between expected and actual benefits should be analysed and captured as lessons learned for future projects.

5.q: What is the primary purpose of the risk identification stage?
o: To capture and record potential future events that may affect objectives
To assign risk owners and set aside their mitigation budgets
To resolve every open issue before project execution begins
To remove all uncertainty from the project management plan
5.w: Risk identification focuses on uncovering and recording potential future events that could affect the project's objectives.

5.q: A project team uses the RACI model to assign responsibilities. Which type of tool are they using?
o: An organisational breakdown structure
A work breakdown structure
A responsibility assignment matrix
A product breakdown structure
5.w: RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) is a common form of responsibility assignment matrix used to clarify roles.

5.q: A schedule is revised to delay a task by three days so a shared specialist can finish another job first. Which technique is this?
o: Time boxing
Resource levelling
Resource smoothing
Risk transfer
5.w: Resource levelling resolves a resource conflict by moving task timings to match availability, even where this affects the schedule.

5.q: The development team reports a defect that is preventing key features from working. How should this be treated?
o: As an issue, because it is already affecting the project
As a change request, because the scope has altered
As a constraint, because it limits the design
As a risk, because it may affect the project later
5.w: A defect that is actively preventing features from working has already occurred, so it is an issue that must be managed and resolved.

5.q: What is regarded as the primary objective of communication within a project?
o: To remove the need for formal project documentation
To ensure that all identified project risks are mitigated
To support shared understanding among the project's stakeholders
To reduce the total number of meetings that are held
5.w: The purpose of communication is to ensure that everyone involved understands the relevant information and expectations.

5.q: A manager arranges a peer review of the team's process to confirm agreed procedures are being followed; what is this an example of?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Scope verification activity
Change control process
Quality control of outputs
5.w: Quality assurance confirms that project processes are being followed correctly so that quality outputs are produced.

5.q: What is the primary purpose of benefits management within the delivery of a project?
o: To reduce the project's overhead costs
To ensure that suppliers are paid on time
To keep the project delivery on schedule
To define, track and realise the intended value of the project
5.w: Benefits management ensures the project delivers measurable value that supports the organisation's business objectives.

5.q: A new stakeholder joins mid-delivery and the project manager uses the communication plan to brief them. Which benefit does this demonstrate?
o: A reduction in the number of technical defects found
Faster processing of change requests through governance
Improved oversight of supplier procurement activities
Consistent onboarding of stakeholders into established communications
5.w: The communication plan ensures new stakeholders quickly receive timely, relevant information and understand existing communication arrangements.

5.q: How does a 'risk' differ from a 'certainty' in project management terms?
o: A risk lies outside the manager's control, whereas a certainty does not
A risk concerns team behaviour, whereas a certainty concerns the sponsor
A risk involves uncertainty, whereas a certainty does not
A risk always leads to failure, whereas a certainty leads to success
5.w: The defining feature of a risk is uncertainty: it may or may not occur, unlike a certainty.

5.q: A team colour-codes its risks red, amber and green to show their severity. What is this an example of?
o: Qualitative risk analysis
Quantitative risk analysis
Configuration management
Critical path analysis
5.w: Ranking risks by descriptive categories such as red, amber and green is a form of qualitative risk analysis.

5.q: During development of the project management plan, which stakeholder is most involved in defining scope and quality requirements?
o: The project sponsor
The team leader
The project governance board
The product owner
5.w: The product owner articulates what needs to be delivered and sets the associated quality expectations.

5.q: What is a key benefit of agreeing a procurement strategy at the start of a project?
o: It removes the need to monitor suppliers once contracts are signed
It gives a structured, consistent approach to acquiring goods and services
It replaces the need to produce a business case for the project
It guarantees that internal resources are always selected in preference
5.w: An early procurement strategy provides a consistent, transparent framework for obtaining resources and services externally.

5.q: A product meets every technical specification, yet customer feedback is negative. What most likely went wrong?
o: The deployment baseline was disregarded
The success criteria did not include user satisfaction
Too much emphasis was placed on iterative delivery
Stakeholders were engaged too frequently
5.w: Success criteria focused only on technical outputs can omit qualitative measures such as user satisfaction.

5.q: What is the role of success criteria when they are set out within a business case?
o: To set performance targets for individual team members
To clarify the benefits the project must deliver to be considered worthwhile
To record the communication preferences of the team
To track the duration of each scheduled task
5.w: Success criteria define what the project must achieve to justify the investment and deliver worthwhile value.

5.q: A team member habitually questions assumptions and weighs the options logically before decisions are made. Which Belbin role does this suggest?
o: Shaper
Monitor Evaluator
Coordinator
Implementer
5.w: The Monitor Evaluator is a logical, impartial thinker who analyses options and offers balanced judgement.

5.q: What is the main purpose of applying resource optimisation techniques when planning a project schedule?
o: To set the thresholds at which changes must be formally approved
To define how the project team will communicate with its stakeholders
To forecast how inflation will affect the overall project budget
To use resources efficiently and avoid periods of over- or under-allocation
5.w: Resource optimisation adjusts the schedule so that resource demand is balanced, avoiding overloads and idle periods.

5.q: Under the communication plan, status updates are issued every Monday by 10 a.m. What does this help the project manager achieve?
o: Freedom from attending project governance meetings
Predictable updates that build stakeholder confidence
Automatic generation of procurement requests
The removal of any need to produce progress reports
5.w: Predictable, scheduled updates keep stakeholders informed and build confidence in how the project is being controlled.

5.q: Which estimating tolerance would you most expect to find towards the bottom of the estimating funnel?
o: Around plus or minus 40%
Around plus or minus 50%
Around plus or minus 25%
Around plus or minus 10% or less
5.w: The bottom of the funnel reflects higher confidence and more detailed information, so tolerances narrow to around plus or minus 10% or less.

6.q: Why is the temporary nature of a project important to the way it is managed?
o: It ensures defined objectives are delivered within a bounded time frame
It removes the need for any stakeholder involvement during delivery
It guarantees the team can immediately be reused on other work
It aligns all delivery activity strictly to the financial year
6.w: Being time-bounded focuses the project on achieving its specific objectives within defined constraints rather than continuing indefinitely.

6.q: A team defines, plans and controls its processes so that outputs satisfy customer expectations; what is the purpose of this?
o: To provide the cheapest possible product to the customer
To shorten the overall project life cycle
To ensure deliverables meet stakeholder-defined standards
To transfer quality responsibility across to the suppliers
6.w: The purpose of quality management is to define the agreed quality requirements and ensure they are met throughout the project.

6.q: On a new IT project you gather requirements, attend progress meetings and support testing. Which role are you performing?
o: Project sponsor
Product owner
End user
Project team member
6.w: A project team member completes assigned tasks and contributes specialist or technical input to the delivery of the project.

6.q: What is the key distinction between a programme and a portfolio?
o: A programme coordinates related projects; a portfolio oversees all projects and programmes
A programme contains only unrelated projects, while a portfolio does not
A programme is aligned to strategy, whereas a portfolio is not
A portfolio is always smaller in scale than a programme
6.w: A programme manages a set of related projects, while a portfolio spans the organisation's entire collection of projects and programmes.

6.q: A project team has reached the adjourning stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership action is most appropriate?
o: Introduce fresh team norms and ground rules
Increase the workload to sustain performance
Recognise the team's achievements and support the transition
Drive the team straight into a new forming phase
6.w: Adjourning marks disbandment, so the leader should acknowledge contributions and help members transition smoothly.

6.q: Suppliers across time zones face delays because responsibilities are unclear. Which core purpose of project management is being undermined?
o: Establishing a clear framework of control and governance
Removing the need for stakeholder input entirely
Delivering the final product without any change
Minimising all administrative overhead on the project
6.w: A key purpose of project management is to provide clear control and governance, including defined roles and responsibilities for decision-making.

6.q: A project manager finds the team has no Monitor Evaluator among its Belbin roles. Which risk is this most likely to create?
o: A shortage of new and creative ideas
Too great a reliance on outside stakeholders
Excessive attention to minor details
Weaker critical analysis and poorer decision-making
6.w: The Monitor Evaluator supplies objective, analytical judgement; without one the team may reach poorly considered decisions.

6.q: A sponsor requests a rough cost estimate while the project is still at the concept stage. Where in the estimating funnel does this sit?
o: A narrow-tolerance estimate at the bottom of the funnel
A detailed bottom-up estimate stage
A final validated estimate stage
A wide-tolerance estimate near the top of the funnel
6.w: The top of the estimating funnel produces high-level, wide-tolerance estimates because little detail is yet available.

6.q: Why is it important that a business case documents its key assumptions and constraints?
o: They define the decision-making authority of governance
They remove the need for ongoing performance tracking
They are legally binding on all parties to the project
They help stakeholders judge feasibility and where risk may lie
6.w: Stated assumptions and constraints let stakeholders assess how realistic the proposal is and where key risks are concentrated.

6.q: A product owner postpones a planned feature so that a newly requested customer feature can be developed first. What does this decision demonstrate?
o: Formal change control escalation
Project risk avoidance
Backlog prioritisation and refinement
Project closure planning
6.w: Reordering the backlog in response to customer value is a core product owner responsibility.

6.q: A senior stakeholder questions whether recent product updates were properly authorised. Which combination of processes evidences both approval and controlled implementation?
o: Change control and configuration management
Scheduling and stakeholder management
Benefits management and procurement
Risk management and issue tracking
6.w: Change control provides the record of approval, while configuration management shows the change was applied and tracked correctly.

6.q: A project audit examines whether the team followed agreed processes. What is the main purpose of carrying one out?
o: To assess adherence to agreed policies, procedures and governance
To assign blame to individuals for the project's problems
To plan the scope of work for the next project phase
To approve the final invoice submitted by the suppliers
6.w: A project audit checks whether project activities have complied with internal and external standards and governance requirements.

6.q: A team inspects completed deliverables to confirm they meet the agreed requirements; which process are they performing?
o: Quality planning of outputs
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Stakeholder management work
6.w: Quality control involves inspecting and testing deliverables to verify they meet the agreed quality requirements.

6.q: In an agile project, which stakeholder clarifies the acceptance criteria and ensures user needs are reflected in the plan?
o: The PMO analyst
The product owner
The scrum master
The project sponsor
6.w: The product owner represents the customer and defines the requirements, including what acceptable delivery looks like.

6.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a change control board on a project?
o: A group authorised to review and approve or reject scope changes
An external panel appointed to audit the project's accounts
A working group responsible for the project's external marketing
A team that decides on the project's team-building activities
6.w: A change control board is the body with the authority to evaluate change requests and decide whether to approve or reject them.

6.q: A team adjusts the start times of non-critical tasks to even out resource demand without delaying completion. Which technique is this?
o: Float analysis
Change control
Procurement scheduling
Resource smoothing
6.w: Resource smoothing uses available float to reduce peaks in resource demand while keeping the project completion date unchanged.

6.q: A finance team updates spreadsheets and processes invoices every day. How should this work most appropriately be classified?
o: Business-as-usual, because it involves regular, repeatable tasks
Business-as-usual, because it has a sponsor and a budget
A project, because it is constrained by time and cost
A project, because it is carried out by a skilled team
6.w: Regular, repeatable work that maintains an ongoing service is business-as-usual, not a project.

6.q: Midway through a project, a client requests several enhancements to the agreed product. What should the project manager do first?
o: Add the changes to the next sprint to save time
Notify finance to adjust the cost baseline
Submit a formal change request for review
Amend the configuration log directly
Update the WBS and proceed with changes
6.w: A formal change request must be submitted and reviewed before any changes are implemented to maintain scope control.

n.4: WBS should only be updated after a change is approved.
n.0: Unapproved changes can lead to misalignment and rework.
n.1: The cost baseline is adjusted only after the change is approved.
n.3: The configuration log is updated after the change is formally authorised.

6.q: A linear project has delivered and installed new equipment and has trained the staff who will operate it. Which phase is being completed?
o: Definition
Handover and closure
Concept
Development
6.w: Handover and closure is where the deliverables are transitioned to the users and the project is formally brought to an end.

6.q: A client wants a fixed upfront cost and schedule for deployment but also wants to evolve features after go-live. Which approach best fits?
o: Extended
Iterative
Hybrid
Linear
6.w: A hybrid approach allows a predictable, planned deployment while retaining iterative flexibility to evolve features later.

6.q: Which of the following is a recognised disadvantage of video conferencing in projects?
o: Prolonged calls can cause fatigue and reduced concentration
It cannot be recorded for those unable to attend
It is always more effective than meeting in person
It guarantees that every participant contributes equally
6.w: Extended video calls can cause fatigue, which reduces attention and engagement.

6.q: External stakeholders report that they are not receiving relevant project information. Which document should the project manager review first?
o: The risk register's list of threats and their owners
The quality plan's checklists and acceptance criteria
The communication plan's stakeholder list and distribution schedule
The benefits register's expected outcomes and measures
6.w: The communication plan defines who should receive which information and when, so its stakeholder mapping and schedule are the first thing to check.

6.q: In what way does unclear authority within a project team present a leadership challenge?
o: It can cause delays and disputes over who makes decisions
It increases the speed of every decision that is made
It removes the need for a project sponsor
It boosts accountability throughout the whole team
6.w: Unclear authority creates confusion and hesitation over decision-making, reducing efficiency and eroding trust.

6.q: A team recognises that a supplier might fail to meet its deadlines. Which stage of risk management does this demonstrate?
o: Risk identification
Risk acceptance
Risk avoidance
Risk exploitation
6.w: Spotting a potential future threat before it materialises is an example of risk identification.

6.q: Which communication method best allows immediate two-way feedback and interpretation of tone and body language?
o: Posting to a shared online drive
Holding a face-to-face meeting
Distributing a printed newsletter
Exchanging threads of email
6.w: Face-to-face communication is the richest method, providing direct dialogue and non-verbal cues.

6.q: A communication plan states that weekly status reports go to the steering group, issued by the project coordinator. Which attributes does this define?
o: The audience, method, frequency and responsibility for the information
The probability, impact and response owner for a risk
The severity, priority and closure date for an issue
The supplier, contract value and delivery date for procurement
6.w: It specifies what is communicated, to whom, how often and by whom, all of which are standard contents of a communication plan.

6.q: A cost breakdown structure (CBS) most directly supports which of the following financial activities on a project?
o: Setting out the responsibilities held by each stakeholder
Assigning individual tasks to named members of the team
Estimating, budgeting and monitoring the project's costs
Monitoring the project's risks and its open issues
6.w: A CBS provides a structured breakdown of cost that underpins estimating, budgeting and ongoing cost monitoring for control.

6.q: During quality planning, a team agrees to follow recognised industry standards to guide development; what does this represent?
o: Selecting the quality measures for the project
Avoiding risk by outsourcing the work
Assigning the procurement roles for the team
Reducing project cost through standardisation
6.w: Choosing standards during quality planning helps define the measures used to verify that deliverables meet requirements.

6.q: Which of the following is typically included in a benefits management plan?
o: The ownership, timing and measurement of each benefit
The baseline schedule data for the project
The list of items excluded from scope
The communication escalation procedures
6.w: A benefits management plan sets out who owns each benefit, when it is expected and how it will be measured.

6.q: A team is building a new mobile app through short development cycles with regular end-user feedback. Which life cycle is most likely being used?
o: Extended
Hybrid
Iterative
Linear
6.w: An iterative life cycle delivers in small increments and refines the product through repeated cycles of stakeholder feedback.

7.q: A senior manager commissions a check on whether a project complies with corporate governance requirements. Which process is this?
o: Conducting a project audit
Planning the project's risk responses
Realising the project's benefits
Carrying out quality control
7.w: A project audit is the formal assessment of a project's compliance with governance, processes and policies.

7.q: A work breakdown structure contains items such as 'code user interface' and 'test module'. What does this structure help to define?
o: The procurement process for the external suppliers
The financial framework underpinning the project
The structure of the client's own organisation
The work required to produce each project deliverable
7.w: The WBS breaks the scope into the work required to complete each deliverable, expressed as manageable work packages.

7.q: Why is carrying out quality planning during the early stages of a project so important?
o: It guarantees the fastest possible project delivery
It removes the need to communicate with stakeholders
It reduces the budget the project will require
It defines how outputs will be verified against requirements
7.w: Quality planning establishes clear verification criteria, reducing rework and increasing confidence in delivery.

7.q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a PBS and a WBS?
o: The PBS defines the deliverables and the WBS defines the work to create them
The PBS defines the risks and the WBS defines the risk responses
The PBS sets the budget and the WBS sets the time limits
The PBS defines the costs and the WBS defines the people involved
7.w: The PBS identifies the product's deliverables, while the WBS defines the work needed to produce those deliverables.

7.q: What is the purpose of the estimating funnel in project planning?
o: To identify the benefits associated with each deliverable
To select the most competitive supplier for the work
To measure the performance of the project team
To progressively narrow cost and time estimates as more information becomes available
7.w: The estimating funnel refines estimates and reduces tolerance over time as project knowledge increases.

7.q: The sponsor asks the project manager to update the delivery milestones in the business case. What does this indicate about their relationship?
o: The sponsor leads strategy while the project manager supplies delivery detail
Project governance is being deliberately bypassed
The project manager holds ownership of the strategic goals
The sponsor is performing the project manager's role
7.w: This reflects appropriate collaboration: the sponsor leads on strategy and the project manager provides delivery information.

7.q: Which of the following best describes how a cost breakdown structure (CBS) supports effective budget control on a project?
o: By setting out the project's overall decision-making structure
By showing the cost associated with each part of the project
By categorising the project's scope into functional units
By assigning named individuals to each of the project tasks
7.w: By attributing costs to each project element, the CBS lets the project manager monitor and control spending against the budget.

7.q: A benefit register entry reads 'annual IT maintenance savings of £50,000 by Year 2'. What does this represent?
o: A project deliverable
A change request
A project risk
A quantifiable benefit
7.w: This is a measurable, time-bound financial benefit that should be tracked to assess the project's value.

7.q: Once a change has been implemented, what is a key final step in the change control process?
o: Monitor the impact and confirm alignment with project objectives
Notify the members of the wider supply chain
Archive all unused change request forms immediately
Submit the change again for a further round of approval
7.w: A post-implementation review confirms the change has delivered the intended benefit and remains aligned with the project's objectives without adverse side effects.

7.q: A project plan shows 'design approved' as a milestone. What does this most likely represent?
o: The list of resources assigned to the design work
The completion of a significant deliverable or decision point
The amount of effort required to produce the design
The total cost of the design phase of the project
7.w: A milestone marks a significant achievement or decision point, such as an approval, rather than effort or cost.

7.q: A review finds a project failed to deliver key elements because scope was poorly controlled. Which process should have prevented this?
o: Scope management
Resource scheduling
Communication planning
Risk analysis
7.w: Scope management ensures that all required deliverables are identified, defined and controlled throughout the project.

7.q: Which of the following would typically fall outside the responsibilities of the project manager?
o: Tracking and reporting project progress
Managing the day-to-day project risks
Approving strategic funding and benefits realisation
Leading the creation of the project schedule
7.w: Approving funding and owning benefits realisation are sponsor responsibilities, not those of the project manager.

7.q: Which of the following best describes a benefit of conducting stakeholder analysis?
o: It improves communication planning by aligning strategy to stakeholder needs
It guarantees that every stakeholder will support the project
It removes the need for a separate risk management plan
It ensures that only internal stakeholders are involved
7.w: Understanding influence and interest allows communication and engagement to be aligned to each group's needs.

7.q: Why is change control generally less rigid in an iterative life cycle?
o: Because iterative projects avoid producing any documentation
Because scope is expected to evolve throughout delivery
Because testing takes place only at project closure
Because the project budget is fixed from the outset
7.w: Iterative life cycles anticipate that scope will be refined continuously, so change is handled more flexibly than in linear projects.

7.q: An office build is estimated by applying a known cost per square metre to the floor area. Which estimating method is being used?
o: Expert judgement
Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Parametric estimating
7.w: Parametric estimating applies a known cost per unit to a measured quantity to derive the total estimate.

7.q: If the sponsor fails to check that the business case remains valid, what is the most likely consequence?
o: Stakeholder support for the project will automatically increase
The project schedule will adjust itself to stay on track
The delivery team is likely to over-deliver on scope
The project may continue without justification, wasting resources
7.w: Continued validation keeps the project aligned to its objectives; without it the project may run on without justification and waste resources.

7.q: Which of the following is most characteristic of business-as-usual rather than of project work?
o: Producing a unique output using temporarily assigned resources
Delivering a defined scope within a fixed time frame
Delivering repetitive tasks and services on a continuous basis
Following a phased life cycle to achieve set objectives
7.w: Business-as-usual maintains ongoing, repeatable services and functions, unlike the unique, time-bounded outputs of a project.

7.q: An app is being built in agile using short sprints, with priorities changing after each review. What does this mean for the deployment baseline?
o: It is defined fully at the start and never altered
It does not exist on agile projects
It is flexible and reviewed frequently
It contains only the cost baseline
7.w: In iterative and agile approaches the baseline is flexible and reviewed regularly as the project progresses.

7.q: Which statement best describes a core feature of an iterative project life cycle?
o: The full scope is fixed upfront and delivered in one release
Formal reviews are avoided throughout the delivery period
The product is released in increments with frequent reassessment
Benefits are only realised once the final delivery is complete
7.w: Iterative life cycles release the product in successive increments, reassessing and adapting the plan after each one.

7.q: In configuration management, what does the term 'configuration item' typically refer to?
o: A stakeholder's preferred method of receiving communication
A deliverable or document that is placed under version control
A resource that has been assigned across several tasks
A task that lies on the project's overall critical path
7.w: A configuration item is any product, deliverable or document that is identified and controlled through the configuration management process.

7.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the project sponsor?
o: Writing the detailed work breakdown structure
Maintaining the day-to-day project issue log
Producing the project communication plan
Approving key decisions and owning the business case
7.w: The sponsor provides direction, owns the business case and approves the major decisions and investment for the project.

7.q: Which of the following would be the weakest choice of project success criterion?
o: Delivery within the approved budget tolerance
Achievement of the required technical specification
Stakeholder satisfaction above an agreed threshold
An improvement in team morale during the project
7.w: Team morale is subjective and not directly tied to the project's deliverables, making it a poor, hard-to-measure success criterion.

7.q: In which type of life cycle is the deployment baseline expected to evolve frequently as the solution develops?
o: Linear
Iterative
Waterfall
Extended
7.w: In iterative life cycles the baseline evolves as understanding grows and the solution is progressively refined.

7.q: Which of the following is a common responsibility of a project management office (PMO)?
o: Providing assurance and support across multiple projects
Owning and controlling the project budget
Managing the scope and deliverables of each project
Acting as the primary user of the deliverables
7.w: A PMO offers governance, assurance, reporting and consistent support across projects or programmes.

7.q: A customer is uncertain whether the final deliverable meets their original needs. Which early activity would most likely have prevented this?
o: Holding more frequent team retrospective meetings
Assigning additional members to the project team
Producing a more detailed schedule as a Gantt chart
Defining the success criteria collaboratively with the customer
7.w: Agreeing success criteria with the customer early ensures a shared, documented understanding of the intended outcome.

7.q: A change in organisational strategy puts a project at risk of cancellation. Who is responsible for deciding whether it should continue?
o: Project sponsor
Project manager
Product owner
Project planner
7.w: The sponsor assesses continued strategic alignment and has the authority to continue or cancel the project.

7.q: A sponsor insists that stakeholder feedback be included as a success measure. What does this illustrate about effective success criteria?
o: They must always be expressed in financial terms
They should include both objective and subjective elements
They should exclude any measure of user experience
They are best defined at project closure
7.w: Good success criteria combine measurable, objective outcomes with subjective elements such as stakeholder satisfaction.

7.q: A sponsor asks how the team ensures their processes consistently produce quality outputs; which process is most relevant?
o: Quality assurance of processes
Procurement planning work
Quality control of outputs
Stakeholder analysis activity
7.w: Quality assurance focuses on the processes used to ensure that quality outputs are consistently produced.

7.q: What is a risk of stakeholders relying solely on written communication such as reports?
o: Reports are the ideal channel for resolving emotional conflict
Reports encourage immediate two-way dialogue between parties
Reports may be misinterpreted or ignored without discussion
Reports remove all ambiguity as soon as they are issued
7.w: Written reports can be overlooked or misunderstood, particularly where there is no chance to seek clarification.

7.q: What is meant by the term 'time boxing' in project management?
o: Fixing the time allocated to an activity and allowing scope to vary within it
Assigning extra resources to the activities with the longest durations
Holding a reserve of unused time to draw on during emergencies
Extending the project deadline to accommodate additional scope changes
7.w: Time boxing fixes the duration of an activity or phase, with the scope delivered varying to fit within the allotted time.

8.q: A defect is discovered while the final product is being tested; which process is responsible for detecting it?
o: Change control process
Quality control of outputs
Risk management activity
Issue resolution activity
8.w: Quality control detects defects through the inspection and testing of deliverables.

8.q: Which of the following best defines a project issue?
o: A problem that has already occurred and requires resolution
A possible delay that could arise during execution
An uncertain event that may affect the project in future
A threat for which a mitigation strategy must be planned
8.w: In APM terms an issue is an event that has already happened, or is happening now, and must be resolved, unlike a risk which is an uncertain future event.

8.q: Which statement best describes the difference in timing between an issue and a risk?
o: An issue is a future possibility, whereas a risk is a current event
An issue is a current or past event, whereas a risk is a future possibility
Both an issue and a risk describe events that may occur in future
Both an issue and a risk describe events that have already occurred
8.w: An issue is a present or past event requiring resolution, while a risk is an uncertain event that has not yet occurred.

8.q: In a project using iterative delivery, which aspect of the deployment baseline is most likely to change frequently?
o: The governance structure
The procurement method
The sponsor's role
The scope definition and priorities
8.w: Scope and priorities evolve throughout an iterative project, so the baseline adjusts to reflect them.

8.q: A new data protection regulation takes effect during your design phase. Which analysis would help you understand its implications for the project?
o: A lessons-learned report
PESTLE analysis
A RAID log
Monte Carlo simulation
8.w: PESTLE assesses how external legal and political factors, such as new regulation, may affect the project.

8.q: Members of a team with mixed experience are in conflict over task ownership. Which leadership challenge does this represent?
o: Slow approval cycles within governance
Inadequate quality assurance activity
Undefined roles and unclear expectations
Poor negotiation during procurement
8.w: Conflict over ownership usually signals unclear roles, and it is the leader's task to clarify expectations and responsibilities.

8.q: What is a risk of overusing group email threads on a project?
o: They always deliver clear and unambiguous decisions
They can overwhelm recipients and dilute the key messages
They reduce the amount of information that is shared
They create an instant and reliable feedback loop
8.w: Excessive group emails can cause important information to be overlooked and reduce overall clarity.

8.q: A linear project finalised its scope during the concept phase. What is the likely consequence when new requirements emerge during delivery?
o: The change will be managed through strict change control
The scope will be re-planned freely at every stage
The change will be absorbed into the work automatically
The team will simply reprioritise its next sprint
8.w: Linear projects fix scope early, so new requirements arising later are handled through a formal, strictly controlled change process.

8.q: What is the main output produced by the quality planning process on a project?
o: A project closure report
A project risk register
A change control log
A quality management plan
8.w: The quality management plan sets out how quality will be defined, managed and verified throughout the project.

8.q: What is the main benefit of using traffic light (RAG) status in project progress reports?
o: It conceals emerging issues from the stakeholders
It communicates status simply using clear visual cues
It replaces the project's earned value calculations
It removes the need for any narrative reporting
8.w: RAG status gives a quick, visual indication of performance, making status easy to grasp and supporting rapid decision-making.

8.q: Why is identifying the critical path important to the success of a project?
o: It enables better control of time-sensitive tasks that affect the duration
It improves the project's overall stakeholder engagement strategy
It determines which procurement options the project will use
It ensures only the most skilled members are assigned to tasks
8.w: Knowing the critical path lets the project manager focus attention on the tasks that directly drive the completion date.

8.q: Several related projects are managed together to improve customer service and maximise value. What are they collectively part of?
o: A portfolio
A business case
A programme
A risk register
8.w: A programme is a group of related projects managed in a coordinated way to deliver benefits not available from managing them individually.

8.q: Members drawn from several departments are struggling with unclear communication and low trust. Which challenge does this illustrate?
o: Difficulties with procurement planning
Cross-functional team dynamics
Work breakdown structure confusion
Disengagement of the project sponsor
8.w: Cross-functional teams frequently face communication and cohesion challenges arising from differing priorities and norms.

8.q: After a change, the team confirms that the new deliverable matches the approved configuration. Which activity is this?
o: Configuration planning
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration identification
8.w: Verification and audit confirm that items conform to their approved configuration and that changes were made correctly.

8.q: Which tool is most commonly used to support stakeholder analysis during project planning?
o: The risk register
The influence/interest matrix
The deployment baseline
The work breakdown structure
8.w: The influence/interest matrix categorises stakeholders so the project manager can plan how best to engage each one.

8.q: A project team is discussing whether their final product meets the definition of 'quality'. Which statement best defines quality?
o: Every project risk was successfully avoided during delivery
The final cost of the product came in below the initial budget
The deliverable includes as many additional features as possible
The output meets the defined requirements and serves its intended purpose
8.w: Quality means the deliverable satisfies its agreed specifications and is suitable for its intended use.

8.q: A stakeholder asks whether the latest test script represents the most current version. Which configuration activity provides the answer?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration planning
8.w: Status accounting records the version history, current status and location of each controlled item, allowing such questions to be answered.

8.q: When identifying the stakeholders of a project management plan, which of the following would not normally be included?
o: An external auditor
The product owner
A project team member
The project sponsor
8.w: The project management plan focuses on delivery stakeholders; an external auditor is not typically among them.

8.q: In a fast-paced project with several stakeholder groups, what benefit does a communication plan provide?
o: It removes the need to carry out any risk management
It maps who needs what, keeping communication relevant and manageable
It guarantees that all communication happens in real time
It automatically prevents any changes to project scope
8.w: A good plan helps the project manager manage the volume and relevance of communication across diverse stakeholder groups.

8.q: When should a project's success criteria be reviewed during the life cycle?
o: At initiation, regularly during delivery, and again at handover
Only once the benefits have been realised
Only at project closure
Only at the start of the project
8.w: Success criteria should be defined early, monitored during delivery to maintain alignment, and evaluated at handover.

8.q: A cost estimate is produced by applying a standard cost per metre of road drawn from industry data. Which estimating method is this?
o: Parametric estimating
Expert judgement
Analogous estimating
Analytical estimating
8.w: Parametric estimating applies a known unit rate to a measured quantity, using historical or industry data.

8.q: In a linear project with scope locked at the concept phase, a client requests a significant change during delivery. How is this typically handled?
o: It is implemented without review to avoid delay
It is added straight into the next delivery sprint
It is deferred until the benefits realisation phase
It is assessed through a formal change control process
8.w: Linear projects manage changes to a fixed scope through a formal change control process to maintain control of the project.

8.q: Which of the following is not normally an activity within the configuration management process?
o: Status accounting
Configuration procurement
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
8.w: Procurement is not part of configuration management; the recognised activities include planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification.

8.q: On a software project the team decides all deliverables must comply with a recognised standard; which aspect of quality planning is this?
o: Creating the change control procedures
Selecting the relevant quality standards
Defining the overall budget baseline
Documenting the lessons learned so far
8.w: Quality planning includes selecting the standards that will guide development and testing of deliverables.

8.q: What is the primary purpose of project management within an organisation?
o: To take over the responsibilities of programme management
To standardise every routine operational procedure in use
To provide a controlled framework for delivering unique objectives
To remove the need for any risk and issue management
8.w: Project management exists to provide structure, control and clarity so that defined, unique objectives are delivered.

8.q: What is a disadvantage of using physical noticeboards for communication on a project?
o: They provide real-time chat features for participants
They rely on people being present in person to see updates
They can be edited and updated remotely with ease
They automatically create a backup of their content
8.w: Physical noticeboards are static and only reach those who can access them in person.

8.q: A supplier misses a key delivery, so the project manager records it and assigns it to the procurement lead. Which stage of issue resolution is this?
o: Analysis of the issue's impact on objectives
Identification and assignment of the issue
Closure of the issue once it is verified
Resolution of the issue through corrective action
8.w: Logging the issue and giving it an owner are part of the initial identification and assignment stage of the resolution process.

8.q: A project was delivered on time and within budget, yet a stakeholder claims it was not successful. What most likely caused this disagreement?
o: The risk register was not kept up to date
The project board was disbanded too early
Lessons learned were not formally recorded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
8.w: Without clear, agreed success criteria at the outset, stakeholders can hold conflicting views of what constitutes success.

8.q: The board reviews every current project across IT, finance and HR to reallocate funding by business priority. What process is this?
o: Configuration management
Programme planning
Change control
Portfolio management
8.w: Portfolio management provides strategic oversight, prioritisation and resource balancing across all of an organisation's initiatives.

8.q: Which of the following is not part of managing a project?
o: Identifying and managing project risks
Resolving issues that arise during delivery
Continuously delivering an ongoing business function
Communicating with project stakeholders
8.w: Project management concerns temporary, defined outputs; the continuous delivery of a business function is business-as-usual, not project work.

9.q: Which of the following is NOT a standard step in the issue resolution process?
o: Analysis
Closure
Rescheduling
Identification
9.w: Rescheduling may be a consequence of resolving an issue but is not itself a formal step in the issue resolution process, which runs from identification to closure.

9.q: In which section of a business case would you expect to find the project's forecast financial return?
o: The quality plan
The executive summary
The investment appraisal
The communication plan
9.w: The investment appraisal presents the financial justification, such as cost–benefit analysis or return on investment.

9.q: Which of the following is a characteristic of scope management in a linear project?
o: Frequent reprioritisation of user stories each cycle
Continuous negotiation of scope with the stakeholders
Formal control of changes once the initial scope is defined
Dynamic delivery of requirements as they evolve
9.w: Linear projects define scope early and rely on formal change control to evaluate and manage any changes thereafter.

9.q: A deliverable is completed on time and within budget, yet the customer is dissatisfied. Which success criteria were most likely overlooked?
o: Measures reflecting the schedule's baseline dates
Measures reflecting the supplier payment terms
Measures reflecting the project's risk tolerance
Measures reflecting user acceptance and satisfaction
9.w: Success criteria should capture user acceptance and satisfaction, not only time and cost, so that the outcome genuinely meets the customer's needs.

9.q: Which estimating method is most appropriate when reliable data from a similar completed project is available?
o: Parametric estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Analytical estimating
9.w: Analogous estimating draws on data from a similar previous project to produce an estimate for the current one.

9.q: A project team has reached the performing stage of Tuckman's model. Which leadership approach is most appropriate at this point?
o: Reassign the work frequently to keep the team stimulated
Revisit the ground rules and reset the team's agreed norms
Provide firm direction and closely define every role and task
Delegate and allow autonomy while monitoring for emerging issues
9.w: A performing team is capable and self-managing, so the leader can delegate and facilitate rather than direct closely.

9.q: A project sets up a version-controlled folder with controlled access for all configuration items. Which activity does this address?
o: Configuration identification
Status accounting
Verification audit
Configuration control
9.w: Configuration control includes the procedures that govern controlled access and the storage of approved item versions.

9.q: Which statement best describes the difference between a product owner and a project sponsor?
o: The sponsor provides strategic oversight, while the product owner manages feature value
The product owner approves gateway reviews, while the sponsor delivers the outputs
The sponsor manages the backlog, while the product owner controls the funding
The product owner owns the business case, while the sponsor manages delivery tasks
9.w: The sponsor secures funding and strategic alignment, whereas the product owner focuses on feature value and customer priorities.

9.q: A developer implements a software change from an informal request, and it later proves incompatible with existing modules. Which process breakdown occurred?
o: Stakeholder mapping was not kept properly up to date
Change control was bypassed and configuration was not enforced
Quality control was applied too heavily to the work
Risk escalation was skipped during the delivery phase
9.w: The change was not authorised through change control and was not verified or integrated through configuration management, so both controls failed.

9.q: Infrastructure is delivered using a linear model while customer-facing features are developed and adjusted during delivery. What is this model called?
o: Extended
Agile
Hybrid
Waterfall
9.w: Mixing sequential and iterative components within one project is the defining characteristic of a hybrid life cycle.

9.q: A target of a 30% reduction in complaint-handling time is set for your project. How does this relate to benefits management?
o: It is a deliverable produced during the project
It is a risk mitigation measure
