It is a benefit that must be tracked and realised after delivery
It is a constraint placed on the project
9.w: The reduction is a measurable benefit that must be tracked and realised to demonstrate the project's value.

9.q: A team has implemented a change, but its effects on cost and schedule were never recorded. Which change control step was most likely omitted?
o: Approval by the project sponsor
Impact assessment
Configuration verification audit
Change request logging
9.w: Impact assessment identifies the cost, time, quality and risk effects of a change and must precede approval and implementation.

9.q: A board has been assembled to oversee compliance, strategic fit and risk exposure ahead of a major investment decision. What role is it fulfilling?
o: Project management office
Product ownership
Project governance
Project team
9.w: Project governance provides oversight, authorises decisions and ensures the project complies with agreed standards.

9.q: You are running a construction project with a linear life cycle and fully defined requirements. What is the correct sequence of phases?
o: Concept, Definition, Development, Handover and Closure
Concept, Definition, Deployment, Closure
Initiation, Development, Execution, Review
Concept, Feasibility, Deployment, Handover
9.w: A typical APM linear life cycle runs through Concept, Definition, Development, and Handover and Closure.

9.q: Which of the following is the strongest success criterion for a new healthcare IT system?
o: Users agree the system improves the patient experience
Every stakeholder is invited to the project meetings
No existing member of staff changes their role
All project invoices are settled within thirty days
9.w: An outcome-focused, user-centred measure such as improved patient experience reflects the benefits the project is intended to deliver.

9.q: During delivery, a team finds that the original success criteria are no longer relevant. What is the best course of action?
o: Abandon the criteria and rely on team discretion
Continue using the original criteria regardless
Replace the criteria without consulting stakeholders
Revise and formally agree the updated criteria with key stakeholders
9.w: Success criteria must stay relevant and should be updated through agreed change control involving key stakeholders.

9.q: What is the primary purpose of quality assurance within a project?
o: To ensure the processes used are effective and followed
To assign the available resources to tasks
To control and monitor the project budget
To inspect and test the final outputs
9.w: Quality assurance confirms that the quality processes used to produce deliverables are effective and being applied.

9.q: A project manager notices discrepancies between the latest deliverable and the configuration baseline. Which process should be reviewed first?
o: Procurement management
Scheduling control
Communication planning
Configuration management
9.w: Configuration management keeps deliverables aligned with the current approved baseline, so it should be reviewed when discrepancies appear.

9.q: After a challenging delivery, an organisation holds a structured session on what went well and what could improve; what is this?
o: A post-project review
A risk assessment
A quality control check
A cost benefit analysis
9.w: A post-project review allows the team and stakeholders to reflect on and learn from the project experience.

9.q: While reviewing the configuration log, a project support officer finds two conflicting versions of a technical specification. Which configuration process has most likely failed?
o: Resource levelling
Risk mitigation
Benefits tracking
Version control
9.w: Version control ensures a single current, approved version is in use, so conflicting versions point to a failure of this control.

9.q: A PMO balances resource allocation and risk exposure across a suite of unrelated IT and marketing projects. What is being demonstrated?
o: Operational management
Programme governance
Portfolio management
Project assurance
9.w: Balancing investment, resources and risk across unrelated projects to serve organisational strategy is portfolio management.

9.q: Which behaviour is most closely associated with strong project leadership?
o: Providing a clear vision and empowering others to deliver
Focusing only on completing technical tasks personally
Delaying every decision until all data is fully confirmed
Micromanaging each individual task within the team
9.w: Effective leaders set direction and empower others to deliver while keeping the team focused on the overall goals.

9.q: A project holds a face-to-face kick-off meeting with key stakeholders. What is a genuine advantage of this approach?
o: It removes the need for any later follow-up communication
It lowers the travel and venue costs for the project
It speeds up the project's procurement decisions
It helps build trust and stronger relationships early on
9.w: Face-to-face interaction helps build relationships, trust and alignment at the start of a project.

9.q: At which points in the life cycle do the sponsor and project manager jointly review the business case?
o: Only once the project has been formally closed
Solely at the point a change request is raised
At project initiation and at key decision gates
Only after the benefits have been fully realised
9.w: They review the case together at initiation and at decision gates to confirm the justification remains valid.

9.q: An estimate for a new school is based on a similar previous school build, adjusted slightly for inflation. Which estimating method is this?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
9.w: Using a comparable completed project as the basis for an estimate, with minor adjustment, is analogous estimating.

9.q: A supplier fails to deliver components on time, delaying the schedule. What is the role of issue management in this situation?
o: To revise the scope so the affected tasks are removed
To document the issue, assign ownership and track its resolution
To plan the resources needed for the next project phase
To reassess the project's future risks and update tolerances
9.w: Issue management handles real disruptions such as a missed delivery by logging them, assigning an owner and tracking them through to resolution.

9.q: Which of the following would you NOT normally expect to find recorded in a risk register?
o: The actual durations recorded for completed project tasks
A clear description of each identified risk
The probability and impact scores for each risk
The named person who owns each identified risk
9.w: Actual task durations belong to the schedule, not the risk register, which focuses on uncertainty and responses.

9.q: A project team has begun openly disagreeing as members assert their opinions and challenge each other's roles. Which Tuckman stage is this?
o: Forming
Storming
Norming
Performing
9.w: Storming is characterised by conflict as members assert their views and challenge roles and leadership.

9.q: Which of the following techniques is most commonly used to carry out quality control?
o: A formal lessons learned report
Inspection and testing procedures
The work breakdown structure
Critical path analysis of tasks
9.w: Inspection and testing are key techniques in quality control, confirming that outputs meet requirements.

9.q: As your project's outputs are handed over to the operational team, what role does benefits management play?
o: It becomes irrelevant once the project has closed
It ensures the expected value outcomes continue to be tracked in operations
It finalises the outstanding contract negotiations
It replaces the project's risk register
9.w: Benefits are often realised after handover, so benefits management ensures value continues to be tracked in operation.

10.q: Which of the following would not typically be the responsibility of a project team member?
o: Providing progress updates to the project manager
Contributing specialist technical expertise
Delivering assigned tasks to the agreed specification
Tracking organisational benefits after handover
10.w: Tracking benefits after handover is a sponsor responsibility, not part of a team member's delivery role.

10.q: A sponsor asks why an estimate's tolerance has narrowed from around plus or minus 40% to plus or minus 10%. What best explains this?
o: More project detail became available, moving the estimate down the funnel
An error in the original estimate was corrected
A different comparison project was selected
A change request reduced the overall project cost
10.w: As a project progresses and more detail emerges, estimates become more accurate and their tolerances narrow down the estimating funnel.

10.q: Which document does the sponsor use to demonstrate the strategic value of a proposed project to the organisation?
o: The quality register
The risk register
The business case
The work breakdown structure
10.w: The business case sets out the value proposition and links the project to the organisation's strategic goals.

10.q: Which process ensures that a project delivers only the work required to meet its objectives?
o: Cost management
Change control
Stakeholder management
Scope management
10.w: Scope management defines and controls the work included in the project so that it delivers only what is necessary to meet its objectives.

10.q: What is the primary purpose of a risk register in project management?
o: To record and manage identified risks and their planned responses
To record the availability of staff across the project
To maintain the project's formal change control log
To monitor the day-to-day tasks of the project team
10.w: The risk register is the tool used to document identified risks, their status and their planned responses.

10.q: Why is it important that project outputs are fit for purpose?
o: To impress stakeholders during the project's review meetings
To shorten the overall duration of the project's activities
To meet quality objectives and deliver value to the customer
To reduce the planning resources needed by the project
10.w: Outputs that are fit for purpose satisfy the project's quality objectives and deliver the intended value to the customer.

10.q: Which of the following would not typically be a project governance responsibility?
o: Scheduling the team's day-to-day working meetings
Reviewing performance against project objectives
Providing strategic oversight of the project
Approving transitions between project phases
10.w: Arranging routine team meetings is an operational matter for the project manager, not a governance function.

10.q: A plan setting out the agreed scope, cost, schedule and resources for delivery, signed off by the stakeholders, is known as what?
o: The benefit profile
The change request log
The work breakdown structure
The deployment baseline
10.w: The deployment baseline records the agreed parameters for delivery, including scope, cost and schedule.

10.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between the project sponsor and the project manager?
o: The sponsor sets direction and governance while the manager delivers
The sponsor manages daily delivery while the manager sets strategy
The two roles operate independently with no formal relationship
The sponsor handles finance while the manager makes technical choices
10.w: The sponsor provides strategic direction and governance, while the project manager delivers the project within those boundaries.

10.q: A charity is running a time-limited fundraising campaign. Why is managing it using project management principles appropriate?
o: Because the campaign forms part of routine operations
Because fundraising is a continuous, repeatable task
Because project management suits one-off, goal-focused initiatives
Because the campaign has no defined end point
10.w: Project management is designed for temporary initiatives with clear objectives and a defined end, which fits the campaign.

10.q: A project manager needs a standard risk register template and guidance on preparing for a gateway review. Which role usually provides this support?
o: The scrum master
The project sponsor
The project governance board
The project management office (PMO)
10.w: The PMO provides templates, tools, assurance and support to help projects plan and prepare for reviews.

10.q: A team holds a brainstorming session to work out what could prevent successful delivery. Which risk management stage is this?
o: Risk analysis
Risk response
Risk closure
Risk identification
10.w: Brainstorming is a common technique used during risk identification to surface possible risks.

10.q: A project manager creates an organisational breakdown structure (OBS). What is the main purpose of this tool?
o: To record the project's detailed work breakdown structure
To show the reporting relationships and lines of authority
To define the project's risks and their planned responses
To set out the methods used to communicate with stakeholders
10.w: An OBS sets out the project's organisational hierarchy, showing roles, reporting relationships and lines of authority.

10.q: Which of the following is least likely to form part of a business case?
o: The investment appraisal
The project rationale
The options analysis
A detailed stakeholder engagement matrix
10.w: Detailed stakeholder engagement planning sits within the project management plan rather than the business case.

10.q: An audit is carried out to assess whether the project's quality procedures are being applied correctly; which process is this?
o: Project scheduling activity
Quality assurance of processes
Requirements gathering work
Risk assessment activity
10.w: Audits are a form of quality assurance used to confirm that established quality procedures are being followed.

10.q: A team member consistently struggles with their workload. How can the leader best influence performance positively?
o: Ignore the issue in order to protect team morale
Remove the member from the team immediately
Provide support, coaching or mentoring to the member
Publicly highlight the member's poor performance
10.w: Effective leaders support struggling team members to build their capability and confidence rather than penalising them.

10.q: A project board rejects a change after assessment shows high cost for limited benefit. What does this demonstrate about change control?
o: It speeds up delivery through early implementation
It removes the need for any stakeholder input
It ensures that only beneficial changes are implemented
It supports uncontrolled changes to the project scope
10.w: Change control applies formal evaluation so the project is protected from changes that are unnecessary or harmful to its objectives.

10.q: Which of the following best describes the escalation step in the issue resolution process?
o: Recording the lessons learned after the issue is resolved
Logging the issue formally when it is first identified
Raising the issue beyond project authority for a decision
Assigning the issue to a stakeholder for resolution
10.w: Escalation is used when an issue exceeds the project manager's authority and requires a decision from a higher level of governance.

10.q: What is the primary purpose of change control within project scope management?
o: To adjust the project's budget in line with the latest forecasts
To allow changes to proceed without approval to maintain momentum
To develop the initial scope statement at the start of the project
To assess and then approve or reject proposed changes to scope
10.w: Change control is the formal process for assessing proposed changes and deciding whether to approve or reject them before implementation.

10.q: What is the main purpose of a decision gate within project governance?
o: To approve the contracts held with suppliers
To assess whether the project should continue
To carry out the lessons learned sessions
To delegate new work packages to the team
10.w: Decision gates provide control points where continuation of the project is reviewed against performance and objectives.

10.q: A team uses a work breakdown structure to define tasks and a product breakdown structure to define deliverables. What is a key benefit of using both?
o: They remove the need to maintain a stakeholder register
They reduce the need for a procurement process
They provide a legal framework for engaging suppliers
They link the work required to the outputs that are expected
10.w: Using both structures ensures the planned work is directly connected to the agreed outputs the project must deliver.

10.q: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates work that would be classified as a project?
o: Answering routine user queries on a support helpdesk each day
Processing the organisation's payroll at the end of every month
Maintaining a client's existing software system throughout the year
Implementing a new customer relationship management system over six months
10.w: A time-bounded initiative delivering a unique output, such as a new CRM system, is a project; the others are ongoing, repeatable business-as-usual tasks.

10.q: A sponsor wants ongoing visibility of progress and risk on a six-month IT upgrade. Which function of project management supports this?
o: Providing structured monitoring and control of delivery
Shifting the project's focus towards routine operations
Reducing the frequency of staff performance reviews
Allocating additional resources to business operations
10.w: Structured monitoring, reporting and control of progress and risk are central functions of project management.

10.q: Why is it important to consider success criteria during the handover phase of a project?
o: To benchmark actual outcomes against the planned objectives
To allow the project budget to be closed early
To reassign the project team more quickly
To ensure the client signs off regardless of delivery quality
10.w: At handover, success criteria are used to confirm that deliverables and outcomes meet the agreed objectives.

10.q: In Tuckman's model of team development, which statement best describes what happens during the norming stage?
o: Members are newly brought together and remain cautious and reliant on the leader
Members work together seamlessly and need very little direction from the leader
Members begin to trust one another, settle into their roles and agree ways of working
Members openly challenge one another as roles and priorities are contested
10.w: During norming, early conflict subsides, trust develops and the team agrees shared norms and ways of working.

10.q: A project passes a risky component to a specialist third party under contract. Which risk response is being used?
o: Acceptance
Mitigation
Transfer
Avoidance
10.w: Transfer shifts responsibility for a risk to another party, commonly through a contract or insurance.

10.q: A team member misses a critical deadline, affecting the schedule. What is the most appropriate response from the project manager?
o: Discuss the issue, find root causes and support recovery
Ignore it and quietly extend the project deadline
Assign the overdue task to the governance board
Escalate immediately to the sponsor for dismissal
10.w: The project manager should address the shortfall constructively, understanding the causes and working to recover the schedule.

10.q: A team specifies tolerances for the appearance, function and durability of a new product; which phase are they most likely in?
o: Quality planning for the product
Formal scope definition work
Stakeholder engagement activity
Quality control of the product
10.w: Defining tolerances and acceptance measures for deliverables is a key part of quality planning.

10.q: A project manager uses a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM). What is the key benefit of using this tool?
o: It tracks the financial cost incurred against each project phase
It allocates the packages of work to their related deliverables
It shows who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed
It breaks the project schedule down into its individual tasks
10.w: A RAM, often using RACI, maps who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each task, giving clear role accountability.

10.q: Which leadership behaviour is most likely to improve team commitment and output?
o: Avoiding all feedback in order to prevent conflict
Withholding key information to retain control
Setting unrealistic targets to push performance
Encouraging collaboration, openness and shared decision-making
10.w: Inclusive leadership builds trust and a sense of ownership, leading to stronger commitment and better results.

11.q: Which statement best defines quality control in a project setting?
o: Training the team members in various quality methods
Planning how the required quality will be assured
Monitoring results to check they comply with standards
Identifying lessons learned from earlier quality issues
11.w: Quality control monitors and inspects project outputs to confirm they meet the specified requirements.

11.q: Why is a communication plan especially valuable during stakeholder turnover or project handover?
o: It removes the need for any formal handover activity
It records prior communications, expectations and channels used
It allows new stakeholders to disregard past agreements
It prevents any future misunderstanding from ever occurring
11.w: A documented plan helps new stakeholders quickly understand the communication structures and the context of what has gone before.

11.q: Why are both change control and configuration management needed together in scope management?
o: To evaluate and approve changes and then maintain them in the outputs
To prevent any changes at all from being made to the project
To provide the project's budget approval and procurement sign-off
To handle only the external modifications made to contracts
11.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures those approved changes are correctly applied and maintained.

11.q: Which document typically captures the details of a proposed scope change before it is formally reviewed?
o: Change request form
Stakeholder matrix
Configuration item log
Communication plan
11.w: A change request form initiates the process, recording the proposed change and its rationale so it can be assessed and a decision made.

11.q: Why are estimates at the top of the estimating funnel less accurate than those produced later?
o: Because the risk register has not yet been created
Because detailed scope and task data are not yet available
Because all projects rely on top-down budgeting at that point
Because agile approaches avoid planning at that stage
11.w: Early estimates rest on assumptions and high-level inputs because the detailed scope and work breakdown structure do not yet exist.

11.q: Which of the following is essential for parametric estimating to produce reliable results?
o: A fully completed work breakdown structure
Accurate historical data for unit costs or durations
Consensus reached through expert judgement
An approved stakeholder engagement plan
11.w: Parametric estimating depends on accurate historical cost or duration data per unit in order to scale estimates reliably.

11.q: Which situation is the strongest reason for a project to adopt a hybrid life cycle?
o: Some parts are predictable while others need flexibility
All requirements are fixed and fully understood
The product is simple, small and repetitive
The customer has minimal involvement in delivery
11.w: Hybrid life cycles are chosen when some components need firm, predictive control while others benefit from adaptive delivery.

11.q: The sponsor has requested a progress report on the project. What should the project manager most appropriately include?
o: Updates on schedule, budget, risks and key deliverables
Strategic alignment assessments and funding approvals
Benefit realisation figures and post-project audit results
Detailed staffing contracts and future hiring plans
11.w: Progress reporting communicates performance against schedule, budget, risks and deliverables so decisions can be made.

11.q: What is a benefit of using several different communication methods on a project?
o: It removes the need to plan communication in advance
It reliably leads to information overload for stakeholders
It allows the project manager to reduce stakeholder engagement
Stakeholders receive information in the format that best suits them
11.w: Tailoring the method to each stakeholder's needs increases the likelihood that information is received and understood.

11.q: Why must configuration management and change control operate together on a project?
o: To assign the members of the team to their delivery roles
To allow the project to eliminate the use of baselines
To ensure changes are properly evaluated, approved and implemented
To remove the need for any formal documentation of change
11.w: Change control evaluates and approves changes, while configuration management ensures they are consistently applied and documented.

11.q: During a gate review of the business case, what is the project manager's main role?
o: To determine the project's strategic alignment
To provide updates on justification and delivery feasibility
To chair the project governance board
To formally approve continued investment in the project
11.w: The project manager supplies delivery information that helps the sponsor present the case for continuation; approval rests with governance.

11.q: Stakeholder analysis identifies a group as both highly influential and highly resistant. What should the engagement strategy prioritise?
o: Reassigning them to a different project
Proactively engaging them to understand concerns and seek alignment
Sending them brief updates by email only
Ignoring them unless they choose to escalate
11.w: Highly influential yet resistant stakeholders must be actively engaged to reduce opposition and secure buy-in.

11.q: After stakeholder analysis, the project manager groups stakeholders for communication purposes. Why is this important?
o: It removes low-priority stakeholders from the project records
It establishes distinct categories of project risk
It creates a new reporting hierarchy within the project team
It tailors communication and engagement methods to each stakeholder type
11.w: Grouping stakeholders lets communication be made relevant, timely and appropriate to each group's level of involvement.

11.q: An estimate based on an industry-average unit cost is challenged as insufficiently accurate. How could its accuracy best be improved?
o: By breaking the work down and applying analytical estimating
By relying on expert guesswork instead
By substituting an analogous estimate
By adding a fixed contingency percentage
11.w: Analytical, bottom-up estimating improves accuracy by evaluating each component individually rather than applying a single average rate.

11.q: Why might a deployment baseline change more frequently in an iterative life cycle than in a linear one?
o: Change control is not used on iterative projects
Requirements evolve throughout the development
Schedules are disregarded in iterative delivery
Project governance is not required at all
11.w: Iterative life cycles use feedback and evolving requirements, so the baseline is regularly updated.

11.q: A previously effective team shows falling enthusiasm and less clarity of purpose. To which earlier Tuckman stage is it most likely reverting?
o: Adjourning
Forming
Norming
Storming
11.w: Teams can slip back to norming when motivation or shared clarity declines, requiring the leader to re-establish focus.

11.q: A manager selects and prioritises all of an organisation's projects to align with strategy and balance resources. What are they managing?
o: A single workstream
A portfolio
A programme
A delivery team
11.w: Portfolio management selects and prioritises projects and programmes across the organisation to meet its strategic objectives.

11.q: Which statement correctly describes a project issue?
o: It is an uncertainty relating to the project business case
It is an unplanned event that has occurred and needs management attention
It is a scheduled event that is recorded in the risk register
It is a constraint that has been imposed by the project sponsor
11.w: An issue is an actual, unplanned event affecting the project that requires management action to resolve it.

11.q: What is the primary purpose of issue management within a project?
o: To develop contingency plans for anticipated external risks
To estimate the overall duration of the project's activities
To record, evaluate and resolve events that have already occurred
To identify and assess possible future threats to the project
11.w: Issue management provides a structured approach to capturing, assessing and resolving events that have already happened during the project.

11.q: When resource smoothing is applied and the project end date must not change, what typically happens to the schedule?
o: Non-critical tasks are rescheduled within their float to even out resource demand
All tasks are moved onto the critical path so delivery is faster
The scope of several tasks is reduced to lower overall resource demand
Additional staff are recruited so that the work can be shortened
11.w: Smoothing keeps the end date fixed by rescheduling non-critical activities within their available float to level resource demand.

11.q: In a project management plan, which role is chiefly concerned with confirming that the delivered outputs are usable and meet the needs of the business?
o: The project governance board
The product owner
The delivery team members
The end users
11.w: End users use the outputs in operation, so they are best placed to confirm the deliverables are fit for purpose and meet business needs.

11.q: What is the purpose of producing a risk response plan?
o: To document the acceptance criteria for the project's final deliverables
To define how the team will react once issues have been logged
To develop the project's work breakdown structure
To set out the actions that will reduce, avoid, transfer or accept each risk
11.w: A risk response plan records the agreed action for each risk, whether to reduce, avoid, transfer or accept it.

11.q: Which of the following best defines an 'issue' in a project?
o: An uncertain event that may or may not happen in future
A technique used to break down the scope of the work
A problem that has occurred and requires management action
A planned milestone marking the end of a project stage
11.w: An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs resolving now, unlike a risk, which is an uncertain future event.

11.q: Why is it important to establish a deployment baseline before project execution begins?
o: It enables scope, cost and time to be measured and controlled
It removes the need to produce a business case
It provides the content for marketing the project
It satisfies post-project reporting obligations only
11.w: The deployment baseline provides the reference against which performance is measured and change is controlled during delivery.

11.q: Which activity is most characteristic of the concept phase within a typical linear project life cycle?
o: Defining the business need and justification for change
Completing the post-project benefit reviews
Allocating detailed work packages to the delivery team
Producing and signing off the final test results
11.w: The concept phase articulates the need, high-level options and justification for the project before detailed planning begins.

11.q: In Belbin's model, which team role is most focused on turning ideas and plans into practical, workable actions?
o: Implementer
Resource Investigator
Plant
Monitor Evaluator
11.w: The Implementer is disciplined and reliable, converting concepts and plans into organised, practical action.

11.q: A plan is being produced to set out how requirements will be confirmed throughout delivery; which process does this describe?
o: Quality control of outputs
Quality assurance of processes
Change control of the scope
Quality planning for the project
11.w: This is quality planning, which decides how quality will be measured and verified before work is carried out.

11.q: Which of the following best describes the role of decision gates within quality management?
o: They replace all other assurance activities
They confirm each phase meets its standards before progressing
They ensure only the final output is reviewed
They remove the need to engage with stakeholders
11.w: Decision gates support quality by confirming that the objectives and standards for a phase are met before progressing.

11.q: Which process ensures that changes to scope are formally approved so they do not adversely affect quality or budget?
o: Risk escalation
Resource allocation
Team briefing
Change control
11.w: Change control assesses, authorises and integrates proposed changes so the impact on quality, cost and time is controlled.

11.q: A senior stakeholder wants to understand how reporting will work across the project's several teams. Which structure should the project manager refer them to?
o: The product breakdown structure (PBS)
The organisational breakdown structure (OBS)
The work breakdown structure (WBS)
The cost breakdown structure (CBS)
11.w: The OBS shows reporting lines and how roles fit within the project's organisation, which is exactly what the stakeholder is asking about.

12.q: A stakeholder does not receive project updates because of a gap in the communication plan. What was most likely left out?
o: The earned value baseline agreed for the project
The storage location of the archived project data
The stakeholder's preferred method and required frequency
The project's formal change control process
12.w: A communication plan specifies who receives what information, when and how, so omitting these details can create gaps.

12.q: What is the result of a leader clearly aligning team tasks with the overall project objectives?
o: Increased scope creep across the project
Reduced accountability within the team
Less involvement from key stakeholders
Greater focus and improved team performance
12.w: When people understand the purpose of their work, motivation and focus increase, improving results.

12.q: Who is typically responsible for ensuring that a project's benefits are realised after its outputs have been delivered?
o: The project quality manager
An individual project team member
The project sponsor or business owner
The project manager
12.w: The project manager delivers the outputs, but the sponsor or business owner owns the realisation of benefits once the project is complete.

12.q: Why might a project manager choose resource levelling rather than resource smoothing?
o: To reduce the number of stakeholders involved in the project
To remove the need for regular progress reporting during delivery
To keep the project's original end date fixed whatever the resource position
To resolve resource over-allocation even if the project end date must be extended
12.w: Levelling prioritises resolving resource over-allocation and may extend the schedule, unlike smoothing which protects the end date.

12.q: Why is it beneficial for a project to establish its quality management approach right at the start?
o: To ensure outputs meet requirements and are fit for purpose
To deliver the project in the shortest time possible
To transfer all quality responsibility across to the suppliers
To remove the need for any project documentation later
12.w: A quality management approach set from the outset helps ensure deliverables meet the required standards and are fit for purpose throughout the life cycle.

12.q: What does a flexible deployment baseline allow a team to do in an iterative project?
o: Avoid the need for governance reviews
Work without any documentation or tracking
Respond to evolving user needs as they emerge
Make changes without any impact on the project
12.w: A flexible baseline lets an iterative team remain responsive to changing requirements while still planning and tracking work.

12.q: A trade union group with a history of resisting change is assessed as high influence and high interest. What is the most suitable engagement strategy?
o: Delay engagement until executive approval is granted
Withhold project documents from them
Assign a junior team member to manage the relationship
Engage them early and involve them in planning to address concerns
12.w: High-influence, high-interest stakeholders should be engaged closely and early to reduce resistance and gain their input.

12.q: A project manager finds that a key resource is assigned to several tasks on the same day. Which technique should resolve this?
o: Milestone tracking
Scope definition
Earned value analysis
Resource levelling
12.w: Resource levelling reschedules activities to resolve over-allocation, accepting that the end date may be affected.

12.q: Warehouse staff who will operate a new inventory system daily are asked to test a prototype and give feedback. Which role are they performing?
o: Project manager
Project sponsor
Product owner
End users
12.w: End users are the people who will work with the project's deliverables day to day and can give practical feedback.

12.q: When is a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) most useful during a project?
o: When defining the project's overall scope and its schedule
When conducting the project's lessons learned review at closure
When assigning clear ownership of deliverables and decision-making
When establishing the communication channels with stakeholders
12.w: The RAM is most valuable when ownership and accountability for deliverables and decisions must be made explicit.

12.q: In which type of project life cycle is time boxing most commonly applied?
o: Linear
Iterative or Agile
Extended
Sequential
12.w: Time boxing is a core practice of iterative and Agile approaches, where time is fixed and the scope delivered is flexible.

12.q: Having developed a targeted engagement plan from stakeholder analysis, what is the next logical step?
o: Cancel all project communications until delivery begins
Implement the engagement activities aligned to each stakeholder profile
Replace the risk assessments with stakeholder assessments
Assign the delivery tasks to the project sponsor
12.w: The analysis and plan lead into delivering the engagement activities so communication stays relevant and timely for each group.

12.q: At a decision gate review, who typically decides whether the project proceeds to the next phase?
o: An external team of auditors
The project manager acting alone
The governance board or sponsor
The project team collectively
12.w: Gate decisions are made by the governance board or sponsor to provide objective oversight and strategic alignment.

12.q: A team member regularly supports colleagues, smooths over disagreements and helps keep the group harmonious. Which Belbin role best fits?
o: Specialist
Shaper
Coordinator
Team Worker
12.w: The Team Worker is supportive and diplomatic, helping to maintain cohesion and ease friction within the team.

12.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of establishing success criteria at the start of a project?
o: It aligns the expectations of the project stakeholders
It removes the need for formal project governance
It guides decisions about scope and quality
It provides clear measures for evaluating performance
12.w: Success criteria support evaluation, alignment and decision-making, but they do not replace the need for governance structures.

12.q: A project fails to meet its key success criteria at a gate review; what is the likely outcome?
o: New scope is added without any assessment
The project may be paused or stopped
The project budget is increased without review
The team proceeds automatically to the next stage
12.w: Decision gates allow the organisation to pause, redirect or stop a project based on its current performance and alignment.

12.q: At a project board meeting, stakeholders are found to disagree on what constitutes project success. What is the most likely cause?
o: Lessons learned were not reviewed
Too much time was spent on procurement
The project budget was exceeded
Success criteria were not clearly defined and agreed at the start
12.w: When success criteria are not defined and agreed early, stakeholders interpret success differently, causing misalignment.

12.q: What is typically carried out during the resolution step of the issue management process?
o: Assigning the issue to a responsible team member
Determining the overall severity of the issue
Recording the issue formally in the register
Taking corrective action to resolve the issue
12.w: The resolution step involves implementing the planned corrective action to deal with and close out the issue.

12.q: When should a project risk normally be formally closed?
o: At the very start of the project's initiation stage
When it is no longer relevant or has been fully addressed
Only after the post-project review has taken place
As soon as it has first been identified by the team
12.w: A risk is closed once it no longer poses a threat or opportunity, whether through response or expiry.

12.q: How does active listening help a project leader to improve team performance?
o: It slows down necessary project decision-making
It builds trust and allows issues to be addressed early
It removes the need for any formal reporting
It promotes a culture of blame within the team
12.w: Active listening creates a safe environment where concerns can be raised and resolved before they escalate.

12.q: Which of the following is typically recorded during the closure stage of issue resolution?
o: The stakeholder responsibility matrix for the project
The proposed escalation route for the issue
The date the issue was resolved and the actions taken
The estimated likelihood of the issue recurring later
12.w: At closure the resolution date and a summary of the actions taken are recorded to confirm the issue is complete.

12.q: Which of the following is true of a responsibility assignment matrix (RAM)?
o: It defines the physical components of the final product
It determines the order of the project's activities
It links organisational roles to the project's tasks
It sets the level of influence held by each stakeholder
12.w: A RAM matches roles from the OBS to the tasks in the WBS, ensuring each activity has clearly assigned responsibility.

12.q: A project team uses a probability and impact matrix to assess its risks. What are they doing?
o: Creating the risk register
Performing risk analysis
Prioritising the lessons learned
Carrying out risk identification
12.w: A probability and impact matrix is a standard method of carrying out qualitative risk analysis.

12.q: What is the benefit to the project manager of defining a communication frequency within the plan?
o: It ensures updates are delivered regularly and predictably
It guarantees that suppliers will meet their commitments
It allows decisions to be taken without any discussion
It removes the need to keep any project documentation
12.w: Scheduled updates create consistency and reduce ambiguity, helping to build stakeholder trust.

12.q: What is the primary responsibility of the product owner in an agile environment?
o: Producing the detailed technical documentation
Monitoring the delivery team's performance metrics
Prioritising the product backlog according to business value
Negotiating and managing the supplier contracts
12.w: The product owner ensures the most valuable features are delivered by managing and prioritising the backlog.

12.q: In quantitative risk analysis, which technique might a team use to simulate many possible risk outcomes?
o: The Delphi technique
MoSCoW prioritisation
An Ishikawa diagram
Monte Carlo simulation
12.w: Monte Carlo simulation is a quantitative technique that models many scenarios to estimate the range of likely outcomes.

12.q: A delivery model of successive product iterations shaped by stakeholder input is best suited to what kind of requirements?
o: Fixed by contract and legally constrained
Simple, repetitive and well understood
Evolving, uncertain or likely to change
Stable and fully defined from the outset
12.w: Iterative life cycles suit evolving or uncertain requirements because feedback between iterations allows the product to be refined.

12.q: Which statement most accurately expresses the difference between a project and business-as-usual?
o: Business-as-usual has a defined end point, while projects continue indefinitely
Projects are delivered by a permanent team, while business-as-usual is not
Projects deliver defined change, while business-as-usual sustains current operations
Business-as-usual delivers unique outputs, while projects avoid any change
12.w: Projects create change and specific deliverables, whereas business-as-usual keeps existing services running.

12.q: A project team recognises potential cyber-attacks as a threat to delivery. What has this activity achieved?
o: It has identified a risk
It has closed the risk
It has analysed the risk's impact
It has accepted the risk
12.w: Recognising cyber-attacks as a possible future threat means the team has successfully identified a risk.

12.q: Which of the following is most likely to be a portfolio management responsibility?
o: Selecting the right mix of projects to align with strategy
Ensuring two related projects are delivered in sync
Monitoring an individual project's risk register
Defining the detailed scope for a single project
12.w: Portfolio management ensures the right projects and programmes are chosen and prioritised to meet strategic goals.

13.q: What is the main purpose of a procurement strategy in project management?
o: To schedule the internal resources needed to complete project tasks
To identify and document the risks that face the project
To define how goods and services will be acquired from external suppliers
To assign roles and responsibilities to project team members
13.w: A procurement strategy sets out how external products, services and resources will be obtained to support delivery.

13.q: Before delivering a major milestone presentation, why would a project manager consult the communication plan?
o: To review the supplier's procurement performance
To approve an outstanding change request to scope
To confirm the audience, delivery method and timing of the update
To reassess the risk thresholds and escalation triggers
13.w: The communication plan defines the who, what, how and when of key information sharing, so it confirms how the milestone update should be delivered.

13.q: A team uses a product breakdown structure (PBS) to represent the end product. What is its primary purpose in scope management?
o: To allocate costs to individual project activities
To estimate the overall schedule for the project
To define the deliverables that make up the final product
To assign team members to each project task
13.w: A PBS breaks the end product down hierarchically to define the deliverables that make up the final product.

13.q: On a rural community project, high unemployment and low digital literacy threaten delivery. These are examples of which PESTLE factor?
o: Technological
Environmental
Political
Sociological
13.w: Demographic and social conditions such as unemployment and literacy are sociological factors that affect adoption and delivery.

13.q: What is a key difference between resource levelling and resource smoothing?
o: Levelling adjusts quality, whereas smoothing adjusts cost
Levelling may change the critical path, whereas smoothing does not
Levelling applies only to Agile, whereas smoothing applies to linear
Smoothing adds team members, whereas levelling removes them
13.w: Levelling can extend the schedule and alter the critical path, whereas smoothing works within float and preserves the end date.

13.q: A project manager is developing a cost breakdown structure (CBS) for a project. What is the main purpose of this structure?
o: To record the issues and lessons learned during delivery
To break the deliverables down into manageable packages of work
To set out the reporting lines that exist between team members
To identify and track the costs of the project's individual components
13.w: A CBS breaks the project's costs down against its components, giving the project manager a structured basis for budgeting and cost control.

13.q: A high-impact, low-probability risk has been identified. What should risk analysis then help the team decide?
o: Whether to accept, avoid, reduce or transfer it as the response
Whether to delay the whole project until the threat has passed
Whether to ignore the risk simply because it is unlikely to occur
Whether to remove the affected deliverable from the project
13.w: Analysis of likelihood and impact informs the choice of an appropriate response, such as accept, avoid, reduce or transfer.

13.q: A PMO introduces a lessons learned process across all completed projects. What is the primary benefit of doing this?
o: It identifies who to blame for previous project failures
It speeds up future procurement decisions
It supports continuous improvement across the project portfolio
It justifies staff changes within the delivery teams
13.w: Capturing lessons learned helps future projects avoid repeat mistakes and adopt proven good practice.

13.q: Which of the following is most likely to support effective communication on a project?
o: Delaying all project updates until the project reaches closure
Engaging stakeholders and delivering consistent, timely messages
Changing the communication approach at frequent intervals
Giving the delivery team only verbal instructions
13.w: Effective communication depends on engaging stakeholders and sharing consistent, timely information.

13.q: What is a key benefit of a communication plan to the project manager?
o: It prevents any conflict from arising within the team
It ensures consistent, structured messaging reaches the right people
It guarantees that the project will be delivered successfully
It removes the need to maintain any project documentation
13.w: A communication plan helps deliver the right message, to the right people, at the right time in a consistent format.

13.q: Why might a project manager create a product breakdown structure before a work breakdown structure?
o: To create a baseline budget for the project
To determine the cost of the individual tasks first
To assign team members to their roles early on
To establish a shared understanding of the product to be delivered
13.w: The PBS clarifies the deliverables required, giving a shared understanding of the product so that the WBS can be built around it.

13.q: Why might an organisation choose to conduct a project audit while the project is still being delivered?
o: To test the completed deliverables for technical faults
To confirm compliance and highlight improvements while action is still possible
To cancel the project before any more money is committed
To sign off the final benefits review with the sponsor
13.w: A mid-project audit can surface issues early, allowing corrective action to be taken while the project is still underway.

13.q: Why are benefit reviews often carried out well after a project has finished?
o: To give the project team time to recover
To reduce the overall costs of the project
To allow benefits time to emerge and be measured
To avoid any pressure coming from the sponsors
13.w: Some benefits take time to materialise, so reviews after implementation assess whether those outcomes were achieved.

13.q: A sponsor asks how delivery progress will be monitored. Which document should the project manager refer to as the key benchmark?
o: The organisational chart
The procurement policy
The deployment baseline
The risk log
13.w: The deployment baseline holds the agreed scope, time, cost and resources against which progress is compared.

13.q: A supplier has failed to deliver a critical component, halting project work. How should this be classified?
o: An issue, because the problem has already occurred
A milestone, because it marks a point in the schedule
An assumption, because it was expected during planning
A risk, because it might affect the project later
13.w: A problem that has already happened and is affecting the project is an issue, not a risk.

13.q: In project management, what is the primary purpose of adopting an extended project life cycle?
o: To shorten the overall delivery timescale
To reduce resource usage during development
To manage post-project benefits and performance
To avoid further stakeholder engagement
13.w: The extended life cycle continues beyond handover to ensure benefits are realised and performance is monitored over time.

13.q: A project's main server crashes, halting all progress. How should this event most accurately be classified?
o: As a risk, because it may affect the schedule
As a constraint, because it limits progress
As a milestone, because it marks an event
As an issue, because it has already occurred
13.w: The crash has already happened and is affecting delivery, so it is an issue to be managed and resolved rather than an uncertain future risk.

13.q: A project manager issues weekly reports on progress against cost and schedule. What key purpose does this serve?
o: It tracks variance against the agreed project plan
It replaces the need for the project brief
It allocates performance bonuses to the team
It approves the project's procurement contracts
13.w: Reporting against the plan identifies variances early, allowing the project manager to take timely corrective action.

13.q: A general election is called midway through a public infrastructure project. Why would a PESTLE analysis be helpful in this situation?
o: It defines the contractual dispute resolution process
It identifies how political change could affect project governance
It calculates the project's critical path more precisely
It improves the breakdown of the technical design tasks
13.w: PESTLE helps the project manager assess political factors, such as changes in leadership or policy, that may affect the project.

13.q: Which of the following statements best describes a typical hybrid project life cycle?
o: An adaptive model that uses only agile techniques
A combination of linear and iterative life cycle elements
An extended life cycle with additional benefit reviews
A series of fixed-scope deliveries with no overlap
13.w: A hybrid life cycle blends predictive (linear) and adaptive (iterative) elements to suit the different parts of a project.

13.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between project, programme and portfolio management?
o: Programme management replaces portfolio management in smaller organisations
Projects are managed independently of any portfolio or programme structure
Portfolio management provides strategic alignment, while programmes coordinate related change
There is no meaningful overlap between the three disciplines
13.w: Portfolio management aligns all projects and programmes to strategy, while programmes coordinate related change and projects deliver defined outputs.

13.q: What is an advantage of using physical, paper-based communication in certain project environments?
o: It prevents any form of miscommunication from occurring
It gives a tangible, lasting record that does not depend on technology
It is always the quickest way to distribute project information
It guarantees that recipients will actually read the information
13.w: Physical communication provides a reliable, permanent record in environments where technology access is limited.

13.q: A progress report shows costs are running fifteen per cent above baseline. What should the project manager do next?
o: Escalate the variance through the appropriate governance route
Disregard the variance because quality remains high
Halt the project immediately without further review
Amend the budget quietly to hide the overspend
13.w: A significant variance should be escalated through the agreed governance route so that it can be reviewed and a decision taken.

13.q: During which stage of the issue resolution process is the effect of the issue on project objectives determined?
o: Closure
Analysis
Resolution
Identification
13.w: The analysis stage examines the severity and implications of the issue for the project's objectives before deciding how to address it.

13.q: At what point in the estimating funnel is a detailed bottom-up estimate typically produced?
o: Immediately after the contract is signed
When the full scope and work breakdown structure are available
After the post-project review is complete
At the initial project concept stage
13.w: Bottom-up estimating requires a detailed scope and work breakdown structure, which are available mid-to-late in the funnel.

13.q: A sponsor wants the flexibility to refine requirements as user needs emerge. Which life cycle is better suited, and why?
o: Linear, because it freezes the scope right from the start
Iterative, because it removes the need for any planning
Iterative, because it supports evolving scope through continuous feedback
Linear, because it copes best with high levels of uncertainty
13.w: An iterative life cycle is designed to accommodate changing requirements, allowing scope to evolve through continuous feedback.

13.q: Infrastructure must be delivered in a fixed sequence, while software features are released in cycles based on user feedback. Which life cycle is being used?
o: Iterative
Extended
Hybrid
Linear
13.w: A hybrid life cycle combines a linear approach for predictable work with an iterative approach for work that benefits from feedback.

13.q: In an iterative project life cycle, what typically happens at the end of each development iteration?
o: The final product is signed off and the project closes
Stakeholder feedback is gathered to shape later iterations
All remaining risks are transferred to suppliers
The business case is rewritten from scratch
13.w: Each iteration ends with a review that gathers stakeholder feedback, informing and adapting the next iteration.

13.q: Which of the following would not normally form part of a deployment baseline?
o: The planned resource requirements
The agreed delivery schedule
The defined scope of work
Benefits realisation tracking
13.w: Benefits realisation occurs after delivery within the extended life cycle and is not part of the deployment baseline.

13.q: A key stakeholder is unaware of a recent schedule delay. What has most likely been lacking on the project?
o: Effective project progress reporting
A change to the project's resource allocation
Completion of all the project deliverables
A fully updated project business case
13.w: Regular, clear progress reporting keeps stakeholders informed of the current status, including any delays.

14.q: Which of the following best describes the difference between an issue and a risk?
o: A risk relates to cost, whereas an issue relates to quality
A risk must be escalated, whereas an issue does not
A risk is recorded in the schedule, whereas an issue is not
A risk is a future uncertainty, whereas an issue is a current problem
14.w: A risk is an uncertain future event, while an issue is a problem that has already occurred and must be resolved.

14.q: A senior executive asks why several delivery options are presented in the business case. What is the best explanation?
o: To provide the delivery team with additional tasks to complete
To satisfy a mandatory legal audit of the procurement route
To evaluate and justify the recommended approach against value and risk
To demonstrate that the cheapest option was selected
14.w: Options analysis allows the recommended approach to be justified on the basis of value, cost and feasibility rather than cost alone.

14.q: How does an organisational breakdown structure (OBS) support role clarity within a project team?
o: By setting out the project's configuration control procedures
By identifying the deliverables that the project must produce
By showing how responsibilities are distributed through the organisation
By detailing the project's individual financial cost centres
14.w: The OBS clarifies who holds responsibility and who reports to whom, improving transparency of roles across the team.

14.q: Which of the following best describes the primary purpose of scheduling within a project?
o: To track the project's risks and open issues
To confirm that the business case is financially viable
To identify the key stakeholders of the project
To sequence activities and allocate time for their completion
14.w: Scheduling sequences activities and assigns durations so the project can be planned and delivered within an agreed timeframe.

14.q: A configuration log records the current status of each controlled item. Which configuration management activity does this represent?
o: Status accounting
Configuration control
Configuration identification
Configuration planning
14.w: Status accounting keeps a traceable record of the status of every configuration item and the changes made to it.

14.q: A late supplier delivery has caused a critical delay. What is the most appropriate first action for the project manager?
o: Notify procurement that the project will be cancelled
Assess the impact and update the risk register and schedule
Escalate straight to the sponsor without any analysis
Reassign the whole project to the product owner
14.w: The project manager should first assess the impact and update the relevant records before recommending action or escalating.

14.q: Which stage of Tuckman's model best describes a mature team that delivers effectively and needs little supervision?
o: Forming
Performing
Storming
Norming
14.w: In the performing stage the team is capable, self-directing and works efficiently towards its shared goals.

14.q: An iterative project has a loosely defined baseline at the outset. How is performance typically monitored?
o: By means of a post-project audit only
Through frequent comparison against the evolving baseline
Against a fixed plan set at project initiation
Against the supplier contract terms only
14.w: In iterative life cycles performance is monitored against a baseline that is reviewed and updated regularly.

14.q: A team member generates many ideas but often loses focus on follow-through. Which Belbin team role does this behaviour most closely reflect?
o: Completer Finisher
Plant
Implementer
Monitor Evaluator
14.w: In Belbin's model the Plant is creative and idea-driven but may neglect the practical follow-up needed to complete work.

14.q: Why is stakeholder analysis important during the planning phase of a project?
o: It removes all project risks before delivery begins
It ensures all project tasks are assigned to the project manager
It identifies stakeholder interests so engagement can be tailored accordingly
It completes the procurement documentation ahead of time
14.w: Stakeholder analysis reveals interest and influence, enabling engagement to be targeted for smoother delivery.

14.q: When developing the communication content of a project management plan, which group most needs clearly defined roles and timely updates in order to deliver the work?
o: The project team members
The regulatory authorities
The general public
The external suppliers
14.w: Project team members carry out the work, so they require clear responsibilities and regular, relevant updates to perform effectively.

14.q: A proposed change is rejected because it would create inconsistencies with existing components. Which process supported this decision?
o: Risk assessment
Schedule management
Quality assurance
Configuration management
14.w: Configuration management maintains the integrity and consistency of the product, so it can identify a change that would conflict with existing items.

14.q: What best distinguishes a project audit from a post-project review carried out after closure?
o: Audits are informal discussions, whereas reviews are formal inspections
Audits apply only to iterative projects, whereas reviews apply to linear ones
Audits assess benefits, whereas reviews assess only the schedule
Audits check compliance and governance, whereas reviews capture performance and lessons
14.w: Audits examine whether the project complied with organisational processes and governance, while post-project reviews focus on results and lessons learned.

14.q: Which estimating technique is best suited when detailed information is unavailable and a quick estimate is needed?
o: Analytical estimating
Analogous estimating
Three-point estimating
Parametric estimating
14.w: Analogous estimating provides a quick, high-level estimate based on past projects when detailed data is not yet available.

14.q: A project leader encourages open dialogue, recognises effort and adapts their approach to the team's needs. What are they demonstrating?
o: Risk-based contingency planning
A purely authoritarian leadership style
Situational leadership that supports performance
Transactional management of the team
14.w: Situational leaders adapt their behaviour to the maturity and context of the team, which supports its development and performance.

14.q: A team reviews trends in renewable-energy legislation to see how they could shape a new facility's design. Which tool are they most likely using?
o: SWOT analysis
PESTLE analysis
MoSCoW prioritisation
Cost-benefit analysis
14.w: PESTLE analysis identifies and assesses external factors, such as legislation, that could influence project outcomes.

14.q: An issue has occurred within a project. Which process is used to resolve it?
o: Configuration management
Change control
Issue management
Risk management
14.w: Issue management is the structured process for recording, assessing and resolving problems once they have occurred.

14.q: Why might a project manager carry out a PESTLE analysis during the initiation of a project?
o: To identify external factors that could influence the project
To map out the internal work breakdown structure
To set the payment schedule agreed with contractors
To evaluate the team's internal communication styles
14.w: PESTLE analysis is used to identify external, macro-environmental factors that may affect the project.

14.q: A project needs a specialised system that only two suppliers can provide. What should guide the selection of a supplier?
o: The stakeholder communication plan
The lessons learned log
The project issue log
The procurement strategy
14.w: The procurement strategy sets out the supplier selection criteria and contract preferences that inform such a decision.

14.q: Which of the following best explains the value of carrying out a PESTLE analysis at the start of a large project?
o: It helps anticipate external influences on the project's success
It defines the individual responsibilities within the team
It identifies the project's key delivery milestones
It estimates the cost baseline used for procurement
14.w: PESTLE surfaces external threats and enablers early, helping the project anticipate factors beyond its direct control.

14.q: A project is undertaken to deliver an output. How is that output most accurately described?
o: A permanent departmental responsibility
A sustained operational service function
A defined product, service or result
An adaptable ongoing support mechanism
14.w: APM describes a project's output as a defined product, service or result achieved within agreed constraints.

14.q: What is a common issue with relying solely on virtual communication platforms?
o: They are vulnerable to internet outages or system failures
They remove the need for any project documentation
They function without issue in every geographic region
They require no training for people to use them
14.w: Poor connectivity or system failures can disrupt communication entirely when it depends only on virtual platforms.

14.q: During a project review, the sponsor asks for an overview of the project's current risks and how each is being managed. Which document should the project manager present?
o: The business case
The product breakdown structure
The project schedule
The risk register
14.w: The risk register is the central record of identified risks, their assessed severity, planned responses and current status, making it the correct document for reviewing how risks are being managed.

14.q: What is a key leadership challenge when managing a newly formed project team?
o: Resolving undefined roles and responsibilities
Delivering specialist technical training
Drafting the legal contracts for suppliers
Avoiding any emotional engagement with the team
14.w: Early in a project, roles are often ambiguous, and the leader must clarify them to prevent confusion and inefficiency.

14.q: A manager defines communication as sending a message from sender to receiver 'with feedback'. Why is the feedback element important?
o: It confirms the receiver has received and understood the message
It formally records the message within the communication plan
It sets out the agreed scope for the project's deliverables

A revised procurement contract for the main suppliers
